move.text: Olivier scrapped the spread of AI coach, insights and voice bets. Voice agents are now Aircall's single core strategy.
move.quote: Voice agent is the future of Aircall. We're going to lead there. We're not going to do 3 or 4 different things

numbers.text: Olivier set voice agents, at a few million ARR, a target of 10% growth a week. They have managed about 1% a week.
numbers.quote: We were a few million ARR and it was like 10%. We've done like 1% a week. Which is not too bad.

broke.text: The HubSpot, Zendesk and Salesforce partnerships that drove growth before 2022 have mostly dried up. Aircall had to switch to resellers.
broke.quote: What's interesting is that today this is gone, mostly gone, because first, what we started with Aircall has become a bit more table stakes.

advice.text: Olivier says keep one core strategy but fund a lab. Air Labs backs four ideas with $1.5 million to test adjacencies.
advice.quote: So it's very important for me that all companies, you have a core strategy, but you need to have a lab.

moments.title: Olivier explains why Aircall's board brought back a founder: AI is a massive disruption and a threat to a phone-based business, and navigating it takes founder-builder conviction rather than a professional CEO's engine optimization.
moments.quote: But then obviously AI came in, and actually AI appeared in 2023, but it really materialized a bit later, right?
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier says the CEO job is now ten times more exciting because AI lets teams build in days what used to take quarters.
moments.quote: And second, it's extremely exciting. Like, yeah, the job I have now is just 10x more exciting than what it was 10 years ago. Like, yeah, all the, like, AI has given us superpowers.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier makes agentic AI fluency a hiring bar, with the interview question 'Tell me about the AI workflows you've built and how you use them.'
moments.quote: Yes, but it's, I know it, like I know it's intuition and I think everybody understands this when you dig into the topic.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier says that even though Aircall is profitable and growing at 700 people, it must change massively because it now competes with fast, AI-leveraged AI-native companies, and culture change is his biggest challenge.
moments.quote: And that's actually going to be the biggest challenge for us. Like, we're a 700-people company. We're actually very successful. We're growing very nicely. We're profitable. We're innovating. So we're not— we don't need to change.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: After three years away from software, Olivier spent three weeks in San Francisco building and training agents and creating his own AI harness, and he wants every Aircall colleague to make that effort.
moments.quote: But there's— we obviously have to refresh our mindset. This is the first thing I did when I joined.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier is removing sequential processes, such as talk to customer, scope, test and ship, and having teams do those steps at the same time because AI makes them fast.
moments.quote: The one thing we need to refresh ourselves is the culture. And that takes time, of course, because you have— we have this inertia of a few hundred people that have been working a certain way and you have to undo.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier says AI is good at cleaning legacy code, so Aircall maintains its core contact-center platform while putting most new effort into building voice agents rather than refactoring.
moments.quote: It's actually easier than one can think. Like, AI is actually pretty good at getting into spaghetti code and like legacy code and cleaning it. So, so we're doing this.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Aircall keeps per-minute pricing for SMB and low-mid-market customers because they want simplicity and outcomes are hard to define, while testing outcome-based pricing, which enterprises prefer.
moments.quote: So they like simplicity, but they like a correlation with the business outcomes. What we see today is that we typically price per minute. It's as simple as that.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier reminds listeners that customers adopt AI far more slowly than Silicon Valley, with many SMBs meeting AI for the first time through Aircall, so vendors should match their customers' speed.
moments.quote: We're selling in a market that's extremely dense, extremely deep. And so we have early adopters, yes, but not everyone has a Silicon Valley company.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier says Europe's main disadvantage is missing compute and frontier models, though voice is an exception with European leaders such as ElevenLabs and Gradient.
moments.quote: So fundamentally, I think we're We're missing compute and we're missing frontier models. So, and that's, I mean, we have what we have, but in Europe it's essentially Mistral. And the compute is massively in the US, right?
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier argues the frontier-model game has largely played out but Europe competes strongly at the application layer, and Aircall aims to be the worldwide leader in voice agents for SMBs.
moments.quote: So I think, like, it sounds like the frontier model game sounds a bit— it has played out. But I think all the application layer, Europe is competing actually in a very strong way.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Aircall's partnership engine with HubSpot, Zendesk and Salesforce has faded as they focus on becoming AI companies, so Aircall flipped to reseller and channel partners who act as mini FDEs configuring its voice agents.
moments.quote: And then there's this third layer that was key to our success, that was the partnerships. So we really exploded before 2022 thanks to HubSpot, Zendesk, Salesforce, Salesforce, right?
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier set an impossible goal of 10% weekly growth for voice agents (they hit about 1%) and told the team to contact the top 500 customers within a week rather than a quarter, because thinking in weeks changes resource allocation and urgency.
moments.quote: So this has changed, but the fundamental DNA, interestingly, and I realized 2 months ago when I came back in New York, And the same vibe came back in Paris, same vibe, same energy, the gong, like the big hairy goals on the screens.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier contrasts a founder with an outside CEO who comes to package and sell the company, saying he returned to build the best product and transform how Aircall works for the next ten years.
moments.quote: I think for me, the very hard challenge is internal, is transforming the company to make it fit for the next 10 years. It's as well something where as a founder, you think differently from an outside CEO.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier describes how fast the market moves, with weekly acquisitions and technology announcements that constantly force him to question his strategy and make bold moves quickly.
moments.quote: And then the second big like challenge I see, I think, is just the markets, the speed of the markets outside of us. It's insane. I mean, it's insane.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

moments.title: Olivier explains Air Labs: alongside a focused core voice-agent strategy, Aircall funds founder-led bets with $1.5M each on adjacent ideas, because you need a core strategy plus a lab when the market moves this fast.
moments.quote: So there's something I have very clear that, that we've set up since I'm back, which is we have a core strategy, like we want leading voice agents, okay, like for mid-sized companies, growing companies, okay, good, let's do that.
moments.speaker: Olivier Pailhès

move.text: Arjun's team chose tokens over new hires. They run a code factory where agents build the software in loops and humans guide from outside.
move.quote: The team has implemented what you call as a code factory, which is the software is getting created by the software itself, right?

numbers.text: From 19 early conversations, 16 wanted a pilot and Docket took 8, unpaid, with a 50 to 60% discount once charging began.
numbers.quote: Out of that, 16 people wanted to get into the pilot and 8 of them got into the pilot because that's all we could accommodate.

broke.text: Buyer attention is Arjun's hardest problem. Well-funded vendors all sound alike, and buyers struggle to place Docket in the landscape.
broke.quote: So buyer attention and their knowledge of where to bucket you in the landscape, that is the most difficult thing today.

advice.text: Be sceptical but experiment. Arjun says the first to make a GTM tactic work gets roughly a two-year edge before peers copy it.
advice.quote: If that thing works for you, then you get a 2-year monopoly or competitive advantage against your peers.

moments.title: Arjun defines Docket as a demand agent that answers buyers' specific questions on a website so they don't have to submit a form and wait days for sales to respond.
moments.quote: Yeah, Docket is a demand agent for your inbound traffic. So the world is at a point where everybody is outsourcing their searches to ChatGPT and Claude.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun explains that only 1% of website visitors submit a form while 99% bounce, making inbound conversion the lowest-hanging fruit in the revenue funnel and the reason he built Docket.
moments.quote: So if you look at the whole thing, right, the whole revenue stack, when somebody is on your website, they are 1% likely to submit on the form, just 1%.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun argues vibe coding can't scale an enterprise-grade company, describes Docket's code factory that cut work from 7–9 days to 1–2 days, and defines AI-native as a product that is useless without AI.
moments.quote: Even today, I kind of, you know, unless you are doing it for some internal app, for like a small indie app sort of a thing, for the kind of use cases that we handle, which is for enterprise and upper mid-market sort of use cases, I challenge the vibe coding thing.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun gives a second test for AI-nativeness: whether the product can tap a company's hiring budget, distinguishing the investor view from the technology view.
moments.quote: Second thing is, is our AI able to kind of get into the hiring budget in a company? The answer is yes, right?
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun proposes a third AI category beyond augmentation and replacement: human-like interactions that were previously cost-prohibitive, illustrated by a Dyson vacuum versus a car showroom.
moments.quote: That's a great question. There are— it's a little bit to unpack there for me. Alex, most of the times we hear about 2 distinct conversations.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun argues that outcome-based pricing only works when an agent is close to a measurable outcome; for long revenue workflows with hard attribution, Docket uses platform plus consumption pricing instead of seats.
moments.quote: Now coming to your outcome-based pricing or the pricing model in general. See, there was the seat pricing.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun explains how Docket found its first design partners: 19 conversations led to 16 interested and 8 unpaid pilots, converting to paid with a 50–60% early-adopter discount.
moments.quote: Absolutely. I believe that for an AI company to go to market, the first set of design partners is very, very, very critical, which is what I also did. I cannot get into a room and build something.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun lists Docket's current top-of-funnel mix: paid ads on Google, Meta and LinkedIn, events, cold outreach, relationship mapping, inbound, and customer or portfolio referrals.
moments.quote: Then from there, we obviously scaled out marketing. So if you ask me today, I have a full engine kicking across the company, right? I have a customer success leader, marketing leader, sales leader, product leader, technology leader.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun says the hardest CEO challenge is winning buyer attention and helping buyers know where to bucket Docket, since AI adoption is less mature than the hype and vendors' messaging sounds identical.
moments.quote: Yeah, getting attention from the business decision makers is probably the most difficult thing now, which is, again, I have to go, which is where these conferences help because they are there to learn.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun tells how VP of Marketing Gary cold-messaged Lucid to partner on an $80,000 car giveaway at HubSpot Unbound within three weeks, and how the car showroom concept tied to Docket's new Showroom agent feature for demoing software.
moments.quote: Absolutely. That was one of the crazy things that we are doing. We haven't given away the car. The contest ends today and it's going to happen in a couple of weeks.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun introduces the marketing factory: marketing leaders and a few people will design assembly lines of self-triggering agents for content, AEO/SEO and demand gen that escalate approvals to humans, rather than using AI only for personal productivity.
moments.quote: See, every marketer who I speak with, they are trying to understand what does future of marketing look like.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun explains GTM skepticism toward AI: AI SDR vendors broke promises and trust by overselling, and AI in go-to-market has yet to reach product-market fit.
moments.quote: Good question. I don't want to put the blame only on the people who are not changing on the go-to-market, right? But let me preface and then I'll come to that advice in one minute.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

moments.title: Arjun's advice to skeptical founders: GTM edge goes to early adopters of what works, so they should test AI GTM approaches like a marketing factory even without trusting them, because the head start can be worth about two years — "be skeptical, but start experimenting."
moments.quote: See, go-to-market is a beast in the sense that if you find something that works, the person next to you is going to start doing it.
moments.speaker: Arjun Pillai

move.text: Emeric is rebuilding Agorapulse's value around Archie, an AI-first tool for content creation and lead generation, because scheduling, replies and reporting are heading to zero.
move.quote: So basically the vision is like, We have to completely change the problem we solve.

numbers.text: Three weeks of model testing cut the gap between a user's voice and Archie's posts from about 40% errors to 12%.
numbers.quote: the post created by Archie down from like 40% of errors to down to like 12% of errors. It took 3 weeks.

broke.text: An X API price increase put Agorapulse at financial risk. Emeric had to lay off 25 people at the end of 2025 and faces three lawsuits.
broke.quote: Financially speaking, like, we eventually had to fire 25 people at the end of 2025 because of that.

advice.text: Emeric says money rarely buys time. Bootstrap until go-to-market and product-market fit are proven, and raise only to scale a working GTM.
advice.quote: But if you are not sure about your go-to-market, if you are not sure about your PMF, money is utterly useless.

moments.title: Emeric recounts hearing Vidyard CEO Michael Litt declare 'SaaS is dead' and push result-as-a-service at an AI conference, which unsettled him about Agorapulse.
moments.quote: First of all, I'd like to share a story with you. A year ago, it was in January, so not really a year ago, 9 months ago, I was in British Columbia in Canada attending a conference, a small conference about AI that Dan Martell was running.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric explains how vibe coding means any basic feature can be rebuilt by thousands of apps and that even complex features are now only weeks from being copied, eroding the complexity moat.
moments.quote: What it has, what has happened since the beginning of this year is that now, and you know that because I know you vibe code and I vibe code too, you create stuff on your own on a Sunday afternoon that would have taken 2 months to a freelance developer a year ago.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric argues that scheduling, replying to comments, and analytics dashboards are all heading to zero value because AI makes them trivial.
moments.quote: Simple and SMB, it's going to be disrupted super fast. Complex and enterprise, it's going to take a little bit more time.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric lays out Agorapulse's new vision: change the problem solved from distributing content to ideating and creating content that generates leads and eventually sales.
moments.quote: So basically the vision is like, We have to completely change the problem we solve.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric explains that Archie only gets adopted if its posts sound like the user, which is why the product team spent 3 weeks on voice testing.
moments.quote: So we asked the product team to go and work on that. They spent 3 weeks testing everything you can test on how we make it sound like you.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric argues that winning on social requires quality and quantity together, so Archie captures everything a user says, from podcasts to lunches, as raw material for content.
moments.quote: The second thing is Archie was conceived to build content at scale. Because I, what I've seen on, on, on social media is that the people who win, they do quality and quantity at the same time.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric explains that volume generates audience data so Archie can coach users toward what works, citing Caleb Ralston's point that nobody knows what good content is until the audience decides.
moments.quote: And the last thing, and we're not there yet, but we're getting there. That's the vision is that Archie, because there is this quantity, and that's also something I learned from the big creators, quantity, he is here to buy data, to get you the data so that you learn what is good versus what is not.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric argues that during product discovery money rarely buys time and adds friction, so in the AI age founders need clarity more than capital.
moments.quote: Yeah, well, I don't need to raise anything. I have €10 million on my bank account. Like, I have already raised money from my customer for the past 10 years, so I don't need to raise.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric says money helps only once product-market fit, onboarding, activation, retention, and go-to-market are working, and is useless before that.
moments.quote: The second thought is money is good when you if you if you have a GTM that works. Like let's let's let's say you have a great product. It does solve a real problem.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: Emeric explains that EOS gave him a recipe for running the company but left gaps in coaching, expectations, and one-on-ones, and that OKRs get forgotten unless embedded in regular meetings.
moments.quote: Yeah, that was a challenge. EOS was really helpful, but then I started to see all the gaps that it does not handle one-on-ones and coaching. How do you coach a team member?
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: After X's huge API price increase in May 2025 put Agorapulse at financial risk, forced 25 layoffs, and brought lawsuits, Emeric started writing his book as a constructive project.
moments.quote: So obviously I didn't have the time. Long story short, in May 2025, X increased the price of the API by a lot. I'm not allowed to talk about it.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

moments.title: On a flight from LA in January 2026, Emeric opened Lovable to vibe code a small one-on-one tool, which grew into My Company OS, the system Agorapulse now uses for meetings, planning, and reviews.
moments.quote: And when the book came out, I say, I thought to myself, this is where things are so crazy. One day I'll need to build a product around the book.
moments.speaker: Emeric Ernoult

move.text: Eléonore treated Pigment as if starting today. She kept the infrastructure and harness, stopped investing where AI now does the work, and shipped agents on top.
move.quote: let's drop the pen. If we were to start Pigment today, what would we do? And we kept the primitives

numbers.text: Pigment crossed $100M ARR after three years of doubling. It has about 650 staff, and 60% of customers are in the US.
numbers.quote: you guys have just crossed $100 million ARR and you've been doubling revenue growth, I think, for the last sort of 3 years.

broke.text: Eléonore says the hardest part is choosing which problem needs her attention, with daily drama over people, processes and deals competing for it.
broke.quote: That's what's hard, is finding the time, understanding where you have to spend your attention, and being able to let the rest go.

advice.text: Eléonore tells founders that bolt-on AI is wrong. Think AI-native, build a moat beyond a wrapper, and innovate fast.
advice.quote: Think AI-native, build your moat, and make sure that you can innovate extremely fast. Otherwise, it's tough.

moments.title: Crespo explains why Pigment keeps its engineering team in Europe, where there is less competition for top talent, while 60% of customers and the executive team are in the US.
moments.quote: So at the end of the day, look, I think the talent, if you want like the best engineers, find them in Europe because there is a lot less competition.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo explains that she saw the cash, revenue and cost planning problem at Google scale, where she was hired to solve it internally, and knew there was a better way.
moments.quote: And by the way, what you describe is very common. So I think most of the time I find founders, as soon as they are very smart and they have the drive, they can tackle a lot of different spaces and it's going to work.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Enterprises can't just use Claude for planning for the same reason small companies could run on Excel: at around 500 employees they need unified data, governance, permissions and scalable complex calculations.
moments.quote: So it's the exact same reason as when pre-Claude, I would say at your size, you could do everything on Excel. It's exactly the same.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo says bolt-on AI doesn't work: ask what you would build if you started Pigment today, keep only the essential primitives like infrastructure and the harness, and rebuild around current model capabilities.
moments.quote: So I think first of all, bolt-on doesn't work. you have to think about an AI-native company, meaning like for us it was, let's drop the pen. If we were to start Pigment today, what would we do?
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Beyond thinking AI-native, Crespo adds two more primitives: build a moat because an AI wrapper is not enough, and innovate extremely fast, trashing and rebuilding features constantly.
moments.quote: The second thing you have to think about that is critical is your moat. And, you know, building an AI wrapper is not enough. You need to build a moat around it.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Pigment's primary moat is hard-to-replicate scalable compute and real-time infrastructure, and the secondary moat is accumulated planning knowledge and customer-specific memory that compounds into tailored experiences.
moments.quote: Our moat is, I think, our infrastructure is what we've spent the first years of Pigment building because it's very hard to replicate.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo advises CEOs not to fight every AI battle: focus first on AI that grows top-line revenue, since other gains will follow.
moments.quote: Yeah, sure. So I think first of all, you know, as a CEO, my recommendation is that you cannot fight on every single battle.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Pigment's AI-first operating model combines a company-wide mandate to be leaner and faster, embedded AI deploy engineers, a centralized team for complex workflows, and a preference for off-the-shelf tools.
moments.quote: Now, clearly, for us, it's been a mandate for the entire company about how can we be leaner, how can we execute faster, and how can every team really use AI to the max and agents to the max in everything they do to operate in a more nimble, agile, and intelligent manner.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo says the goal is to become leaner every year, framing it not as having too many people but as staying agile and innovating fast, as AI-native customers like Vercel, Glean and Anthropic do with small finance teams.
moments.quote: Yeah, great question. So I think definitely like the goal for us is to become leaner and leaner and leaner every year. And this is what we do with our customers.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo explains the co-CEO model: clearly defined roles (her co-founder leads product, technology and HR; she leads everything else) and constant communication that closes the loop between business and product.
moments.quote: Yeah, so we've always been 2 CEOs. We are both co-founders of the company. cannot work better for us. I think that really depends on the team, on your co-founder, on your own mentality, on your own personality.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: The first growth driver is an impeccable enterprise sales machine: shorter sales cycles, tight lead qualification, lean operations and fast account-executive ramp-up.
moments.quote: Yeah, so it's a combination of things. So if I start, where should I start? Maybe I could start by the go-to-market side and then product.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo completes her growth flywheel: better sales cycles and switching, brand and community building, and above all fast product innovation that brings AI to customers on a silver platter.
moments.quote: So that's the first thing, really improving your sales cycle, your ability to switch from players. The second is making noise, marketing everywhere.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Pigment's free trial lets prospects vibe-code an enterprise app in minutes, reducing buying friction and sales cycles in a category historically sold through long, high-touch processes.
moments.quote: Yeah, and that goes into my first point, which is how do you remove the friction for people to buy? And so what we realize is that we have an amazing technology.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Crespo tells early-stage founders that business planning is a must-have, not a nice-to-have, and that like Formula 1 teams, the companies that optimize most win, so they shouldn't wait to start.
moments.quote: I think first of all, it's essential. It's not a nice-to-have, it's a must-have because it's the only way for you to improve your top line and your costs in a very efficient manner.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

moments.title: Excel remains fine for ad hoc analysis, but Crespo argues scalable planning processes shouldn't run on spreadsheets, and her best customers, like L'Oréal, say they could never go back.
moments.quote: Let's get the crystal ball out. In 2028, are finance teams, business planners still going to be using Excel for business planning? I think if they do, again, they are not in the right game.
moments.speaker: Eléonore Crespo

move.text: Alex stopped Groove signups at $4.5M ARR and shut Helply V1, rebuilding an agentic support platform because the moat is proprietary data.
move.quote: the moat isn't like that chatbot that sits on your site. The moat is the proprietary data.

numbers.text: At $5M ARR, Groove had 99% NRR and 90% logo retention but averaged only 25 new customers a month, fewer than it was losing.
numbers.quote: the catch for us was we were averaging only 25 new customers a month for our SaaS.

broke.text: The $500 deposits did not hold everyone, and Alex admits some pre-sold customers have gone. He says the rebuild is still unproven.
broke.quote: It's only a $500 deposit. Um, have we lost some customers? For sure.

advice.text: Alex tells founders to design for AI plus a human, not bolt AI onto human workflows, and to avoid his route of acquisitions and new brands.
advice.quote: Is your platform designed for AI plus a human, not human plus AI? Because human plus AI is just bolting on AI.

moments.title: Alex frames the Groove-to-Helply decision as creative destruction: a 15-year, $5M ARR bootstrapped legacy help desk was killed to start over for the agentic era.
moments.quote: We've had a legacy help desk solution called Groove, our prior company Groove, now rebranded to Helply for 15 years in the marketplace.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Alex explains Jason Lemkin's NRR zombie definition: $2M-$20M ARR, 90-100% NRR, 80-90% logo retention, but an inability to acquire new customers.
moments.quote: at, as, as it relates to our growth in 2024 as we're hitting $5 million ARR, throughout that year we're seeing signs of Groove becoming what Jason Lemkin referred to as a net revenue retention zombie.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Alex argues legacy SaaS is fighting an uphill battle, and that falling seat counts and seat-based pricing were killing Groove between 2023 and 2026.
moments.quote: And. And now it's completely agentic, right? It's kind of transformed into a completely new era of software, AI-native. And if you're a legacy SaaS, I truly believe that you're fighting an uphill battle.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: In May 2024 Alex wrote to a former business partner that avoiding the NRR zombie stage required rebooting the product, brand and GTM strategy entirely.
moments.quote: And I sent out a note to a former business partner and I said, listen, the only way that we're not going to really like sink ourselves into this NRR zombie stage is if we completely, completely reboot the product, reboot the brand, and then also reboot our GTM strategy.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Bolting AI drafts and edits onto Groove produced only minor efficiency gains because a human was still clicking around.
moments.quote: So we had started customer development, like first, even before Helply with Groove, we, we bolted on AI onto Groove. Right? Those are the simple things like AI drafts, AI edits.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Helply V1, an agnostic AI chatbot sold as an add-on to Groove customers, reached 252 paying customers and $1M ARR with strong tier-1 deflection results.
moments.quote: At the same time, our our our attempt two was doing a lot of customer development around what is now Helply.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Alex argues a paradigm shift is underway: software and subscriptions persist, but customers increasingly buy the work performed rather than access to tools, and AI performance replaces human measurement.
moments.quote: And then there's the measurement piece of it where you're not measuring humans anymore, you're measuring the performance and the outcomes of of AI.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: After stopping Groove signups and Helply V1, Alex concludes the moat is not a chatbot on your site but proprietary data, which you only get by owning the customer's data rather than integrating with Zendesk.
moments.quote: In 2025, in September, as we're looking at the landscape, we end up starting literally everything from scratch again. All right.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Having tried bolt-ons and a drastic V1 experiment, the team rebuilt a fully agentic support platform from the ground up, with workflows designed for AI with a human rather than a human using AI.
moments.quote: So we kind of stepped back and said, all right, what, like we've experimented with bolting on AI into Groove. We did this really drastic experiment with Helply version 1.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Alex plans to migrate all 1,400 Groove customers to Helply V2 through 2027, having learned that maintaining two products as a small company is basically impossible.
moments.quote: Yes, for sure. And all of the Groove customer base will eventually be migrated over into, into Helply version 2 the new agentic complete customer support platform.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Alex says he loves competition because it signals demand, noting the space is more crowded than he has ever seen, with six vendors beside Helply at a recent event.
moments.quote: Getting back to your question around like the competition though. Yes, there's competition, right? But again, I've always had this notion where I love competition. I love competition. I think it signals like there's demand in the space.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Seat-based incumbents like Intercom can't drop seats without a 30-40% MRR hit, so bootstrapped Helply can go seatless and charge only for AI work.
moments.quote: Now, the way that we look at that too is Getting back to AI, how are you going— like, in terms of pricing, how are you going to, to, to look at the landscape with all of your incumbents that are seat-based?
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Alex warns other founders not to copy his path of acquisitions, new brands and a full rebuild, calling it an extreme risk that he hasn't yet proven.
moments.quote: So I did it in kind of a, a really twisted way. whether or not it was through acquisitions, through coming up with new brands, like, don't do that, right?
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Legacy SaaS founders should ask whether their platform is designed for AI plus a human or human plus AI: bolt-ons are the latter, while AI-first designs experience, workflows and pricing around AI.
moments.quote: I do believe Legacy SaaS for sure has to think about making the hard decisions around: Is your platform designed for AI plus a human, not human plus AI? Because human plus AI is just bolting on AI.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

moments.title: Because AI lets teams code far faster, now is arguably the best time in SaaS history to greenfield a rebuild, though founders should ask whether others can vibe code them out and whether their pricing is right.
moments.quote: AI is going to help you do it ten x more efficiently. With with now the the ability to code like. 10 times faster.
moments.speaker: Alex Turnbull

move.text: Jacco bets that for the next two years human-to-human connection will dominate business, with high-touch sales run by humans aided by AI.
move.quote: the human-to-human connection is more important than ever. And over the next 2 years, it will be the dominant factor

numbers.text: As Jacco tells it, Airtable and Miro, both valued at $7 billion and above, sold to the same buyer within 5 weeks for $1 billion and change.
numbers.quote: both in 5 weeks by the same company, both valued at $7 billion and above, selling for $1 billion and change.

broke.text: Jacco admits products and services Winning by Design built six months ago are already obsolete. He also warns AI companies are repeating SaaS's inbound dependency.
broke.quote: Products and services that we at Winning by Design built 6 months ago are obsolete at this point in time.

advice.text: Jacco tells founders to list their five or six main constraints, ask AI what causes them, then use AI to remove them rather than automating old processes.
advice.quote: if you line them all up, you say like, what are the 5 or 6 main constraints that are holding me back?

moments.title: Jacco says AI companies are repeating the mistakes that sank SaaS, only faster, with effects from 2027, and that AI did not cause SaaS's problems but exposed them.
moments.quote: I think of them as software companies, and there's different kinds of software companies. Hard to extract who is SaaS and AI. I think that's one.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco recalls warning the industry at SaaStock in 2018-19 and argues the repeat is preventable, especially for a more reasonable European audience.
moments.quote: What I mean with that is that AI actually can be the solution to many of the problems that we have run into in SaaS.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco outlines a constraint-first approach to AI: list the 5-6 main constraints, ask AI for their causes, and use it to eliminate them rather than for spam or SDR replacement, which is like using a Ferrari as a lawnmower.
moments.quote: Yeah, the main realization that we need to have is that AI can help lots of the problems historically that were the constraints to our business.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco argues no individual has all the answers about AI, so practitioners should learn and test together in communities rather than as individualists.
moments.quote: Now, my big thing of that, Alex, and what you have always done over the years is this. No single person has all the knowledge on this.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco says the timing matters: it is hard to project even 3-6 months ahead, and a new season of gatherings beyond Dreamforce-style enthusiasm is needed.
moments.quote: Second thing I wanna point out to you, It's the timing, Alex. The timing is so important.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco urges leaders to bring colleagues to AI events because the topic touches every function: better one event with 2-3 people than three events with one person.
moments.quote: Many organizations— there's another thing I want to bring up, you know, like, and we see the importance of this, Aleks. I want people to hear this video and say, don't come alone.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco predicts human-to-human connection will be the dominant factor in business for the next two years and splits sales into high-touch (humans aided by AI) and high-volume (AI aided by humans).
moments.quote: That the way moving forward is not sales will be replaced by AI. The way moving forward is that the human-to-human connection is more important than ever.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco tells anxious leaders to calm down and focus AI on a few basics, and pushes back on AI doom by arguing people have a choice in what to make of it.
moments.quote: And I'm sitting here in front of us. How many people, Alex, don't sit right now in a cubicle listening to this and going like, I'm panicking. What do I need to be doing?
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

moments.title: Jacco explains AI GTM tools underperform because they're applied to old processes, and warns the inbound-dependent model built over 15 years, now being repeated by AI companies, will break.
moments.quote: Alex, the reason why that is because we're applying AI to old processes. If we apply AI to old processes, they will do what old processes do, but arguably at a lower cost and at a bigger scale.
moments.speaker: Jacco van der Kooij

move.text: Krzysztof argues against a 180-degree switch to usage pricing. He favours hybrid models, testing usage metrics through add-ons or bundles on top of seats.
move.quote: Nevertheless, making it all at once, shifting it, shift, shifting it 180 degrees is very rarely a good idea.

numbers.text: Krzysztof says 95% of Valueships engagements end with a price increase. Its surveys cover 40 to 50 companies a year.
numbers.quote: 95% of our engagements ends up with increase of the price. So if you have guesstimated your price, most likely you are charging too low.

broke.text: One of Krzysztof's clients went full usage on its own. The value and revenue case held up, but users were not prepared to accept it.
broke.quote: Apparently, unfortunately for them, users were not prepared for that, right? So they were not accepting to be charged for the things

advice.text: Krzysztof tells founders to align price with the value they deliver, test on existing customers first and treat pricing as a continuous process.
advice.quote: understand on easy battleground, which is your currently existing clients, how the pricing process can look like, and then start working on your pricing.

moments.title: The most expensive SaaS pricing mistake is not treating pricing as an ongoing process, even though volume and costs get continuous attention and pricing is usually a one-off 10% increase every three years.
moments.quote: So not treating pricing as a process. I think that this is my— if there is one, this is the one. So think about this, right? I mean, price is a profit slash growth lever, right?
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Companies rarely have even 1.2 FTE responsible for pricing, so a lack of capability and responsibility makes them afraid of it.
moments.quote: So a couple of points. The first one that you mentioned, 100%. Rarely there is a person or like even 1.2 FTE that is responsible for pricing. So that's number one.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Pricing is a leaky bucket, like a disease, because suboptimal pricing does not kill a company fast but quietly cuts the effect of every sales, marketing, and product investment.
moments.quote: The third one, and I think this is also quite important, you know, pricing is very rarely, or used to be, and now it's much different, but used to be rarely a burning thing, right?
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Valueships treats pricing as an engineering exercise, drawing on a technology-only client base, a benchmark and pricing-page knowledge base, and constant industry learning.
moments.quote: So first of all, we treat pricing as an engineering exercise. So one advantage that we do have is like the database and all the experience that we are having working across multiple industries within technology.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: The AI era merges the custom-software and cloud/SaaS eras by tailoring a platform to each client through agents, which eventually pushes pricing toward a per-client model.
moments.quote: Then we realized maybe this is not needed. We moved into the cloud era, which means that we were much faster, cheaper, but we were solving, let's say, 70-80% of the problems that our clients were having.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Despite the hype about outcome-only pricing, survey data shows buyers still prefer hybrid models with usage on top of classic SaaS metrics, so companies should avoid an abrupt 180-degree switch from seats to usage-only.
moments.quote: If you take all of them into consideration and if you zoom out from the LinkedIn noise or from the buzz, Of course, maybe not of course, but majority of the marketing buzz is telling us that you should move from seats and now we should also only charge per output or outcome.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Instead of switching everything at once, test alternative value metrics in a new add-on or bundle, since buyers are increasingly open to metrics other than seats.
moments.quote: So I would say that first of all, understand your revenue and how changing the value metric can influence your revenue and then implement cadence, right?
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Choosing a value metric works as a shortlisting funnel: check technical feasibility, check correlation with customer value, then assess the impact on current users.
moments.quote: So I don't want to be very boring here, but I see a lot of companies battling their technological debt. So first of all, you need to understand what usage metrics are actually feasible to charge.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Before rolling out a new usage metric, model its effect on churn, conversion, and cash flow, then start with beta testers or a new product or add-on.
moments.quote: So like if you would like to migrate them or move them to the usage-based plans, how it's going to influence your churn, how it's going to influence your conversion, right?
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: A client went full usage pricing to follow the industry; the value logic and analytics were sound, but customers refused to pay for the chosen metric, so the implementation failed.
moments.quote: Recently, I had a client situation where one of my clients basically decided They decided by themselves that they are going full usage because industry is heading that way.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: The first steps of a pricing process are to align pricing with company strategy and define the financial KPI to improve, such as margin or NRR.
moments.quote: You can increase your prices if you want to boost your margin, which brings me to the answer to your question, which is Pricing is a horizontal function that needs to be aligned with the strategic goals of your company, which means that the first part of the process is actually understanding what we want to achieve, right?
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: A pricing test might raise prices for the 10% of clients paying below the median for equal value, then scale if it works and kill if it doesn't, within a four-step process.
moments.quote: Then understand what you want to achieve. Then typically you design the test, right? So you want to Boost your revenue from currently existing clients.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: AI-native startups should differentiate packages rather than use one all-in-one price, because even two plans reveal what drives willingness to pay, and 80% of customers on the top plan signals underpricing.
moments.quote: So if you're just starting, I would say, and There is— I had a big battle over again LinkedIn on that. So, you know, I don't own the truth. Take your magnifying glass to what I'm preaching.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Valueships' research found that companies with a core value metric plus one or two supporting metrics tend to charge more for the same value proposition, so hybrid models often lift willingness to pay.
moments.quote: Through our research, we also Nowadays, see that companies that are having more than one CVM, so like you know core value metric.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: The AI era feels ADD-like, with priorities shifting between pricing, LLM searchability, and AI SDRs, so teams need to filter noise through a revenue lens.
moments.quote: Secondly, And this is going to be a very not pricing related, but in general horizontal technology takeaway. I have the feeling that we are like in the very ADD type of a situation right now.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Seats worked as a pricing metric because humans were the measurement system for value, but AI agents break that link between users and output.
moments.quote: TL;DR, no. Adding a bit of a context to it, I think it's important to understand why all of this is happening, right? And I think this is all about the measurement system.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Seats will persist where AI only supports humans or where legal, compliance, or hardware barriers are high, and will be at risk where AI can replace humans easily; companies should weigh human replaceability and workflow penetration.
moments.quote: So that brings me to my point that for softwares that are very commoditized, for the industries that do have a high entry barrier from the legal standpoint, That for companies that are utilizing hardware plus software, suddenly they're very cool because the barrier of entry to challenge them is quite high.
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

moments.title: Asked what a founder should do this week, Krzysztof notes that 95% of engagements end in a price increase, so founders should align price with value, test on existing clients, and adopt #AlwaysWorkOnPricing.
moments.quote: Final question, Chris. So there's a founder that's listening to this. They suspect their pricing is wrong for the AI era. They don't know where to start. What's one thing you would tell them to do this week?
moments.speaker: Krzysztof Szyszkiewicz

move.text: St John's Perlon automates the first touch only. Once a prospect replies, humans take over, and the built-in dialer is human, not AI.
move.quote: once a prospect responds to one of the messages across whichever platform it might be, that's over to the humans to take up that conversation

numbers.text: Perlon's own platform generates about 70% of its new business. St John says that has taken the company to seven figures and above in ARR.
numbers.quote: So the Perlon platform generates about 70% of our new business. We use our platform at scale and we test a lot.

broke.text: St John's hardest problem is change management. Customers say they want AI, then will not commit the time to train and iterate.
broke.quote: But when it comes down to it, like actually attributing the time and getting them to do that, that's the hardest part.

advice.text: If outbound is failing, St John says go manual first. Pick 200 dream accounts, write bespoke messages, learn what lands, then automate.
advice.quote: Isolate 200 customers that you would absolutely love to work with if you could work with any 200 customers, and then start doing things manually.

moments.title: Dalgleish says AI SDRs have mostly failed so far because the tools started out basic and teams haven't invested the testing and iteration needed, since they are not plug-and-play pipeline generators.
moments.quote: So I think the short answer to that for most companies so far has been no.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish compares an AI SDR tool to a new hire that needs training, and recommends assigning one senior owner who gets into the weeds and is accountable for refining it.
moments.quote: Yeah, absolutely. And I think the equivalent is bring on a new hire, right? You're not just going to throw a new hire into the mix and say, you know, good luck.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish explains that short CRO/VP Sales tenures and pressure for fast results clash with the patience needed to train an AI outbound tool, so expectation setting is part of selling it.
moments.quote: I think the problem as well that we kind of see is that sales by nature, and if you look at like the CRO or the VP of sales role, the average tenure of these roles is usually about a year and a half.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish describes how his outbound-team background and his co-founder's ML expertise led from the Perlon Labs AI consultancy to the first basic version of Perlon AI.
moments.quote: Yeah, so my background was in building and sort of running outbound teams. I'd spent 4 or 5 years doing this specifically in the pre sort of AI age where my focus had always been telling our teams to write hyper-personalized, really, really well-researched messages.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Perlon's first customer was a UK private-jet broker whose need for hyper-relevant messages shaped the product, and after a few aviation customers an inbound investor email led them to take a small check and focus on product.
moments.quote: So yeah, we sold it to one client in the UK. they were a private jet broker, so they were reaching out to ultra-high net worths.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: After signing a crypto-compliance customer, the founders realized outbound works broadly the same way across industries, making Perlon a horizontal platform.
moments.quote: The third customer, sorry, the fourth customer that we sold it into was a crypto compliance business.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish says Perlon hands every reply to humans and offers only a human dialer, arguing the best teams combine AI-run email and LinkedIn with humans on the phone and in meetings.
moments.quote: Yeah, we very much see it as the fact that sales teams are still going to be needed. You still need these humans.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish outlines an account-tiering model: tier-1 accounts get fully human outreach while the long tail runs through automation, and the human salesperson isn't going anywhere.
moments.quote: So I think that's it. The SDR role, you know, shouldn't really be doing much that's text-based. Apart from for your like absolute tier 1 accounts.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish argues AI cold-calling isn't ready, since many recipients can't tell it's an AI and a brand selling $100K+ products shouldn't trust an AI to make the first call to a senior buyer.
moments.quote: So that's it. I think with these AI calls, I don't think the world is really ready for them. And I don't think many people are prepared to be sold to by an AI at this stage.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Responding to the saturation concern, Dalgleish says GTM must be multifaceted and that email and LinkedIn are noisy mainly because of bad, scraped AI messages, so well-contextualized outreach cuts through.
moments.quote: So I think any GTM strategy and any salesperson's outbound strategy needs to be multifaceted and have every kind of angle covered, right?
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish argues legacy platforms like HubSpot, Outreach and SalesLoft bolted AI onto products not built for agentic outbound, with limited scale and customization of research agents.
moments.quote: Yeah. So I think a lot of the old-school kind of tools Have tried to bolt on AI features to to what they do. So, you know, the likes of HubSpot, the likes of Outreach, SalesLoft, etc.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish says an AI-native platform puts contact data, mailbox architecture, LinkedIn automation and a dialer under one roof so an agent can operate the whole outbound stack.
moments.quote: That is key because if we look at our product, so we've got everything from contact data to mailbox architecture to LinkedIn automation to a dialer. Everything that you need to run outbound is under one roof.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: The most wrong claim Dalgleish hears is that AI in sales doesn't work; digging in usually reveals insufficient testing, iteration and team adoption.
moments.quote: The most, I'd say, I'd say it's just that it doesn't work. Yeah, it doesn't work, you know? And it's like, okay, well, let's have a look at what you've done.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish urges skeptics to revisit AI GTM tools by comparing how far LLMs have come in two years, especially before deciding to hire more salespeople.
moments.quote: I think it's very much the same with, with GTM. I think a lot of people maybe did dip their toe in in the early days when these tools sucked.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish says customers measure ROI through reply rates, warm leads, meetings booked and pipeline, plus the selling time returned to SDRs, with expectations depending on ticket size.
moments.quote: So a lot of our customers will really kind of look at the sort of core metrics. So those are going to be things like reply rates, number of meetings booked.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish says Perlon pairs every customer with a customer success manager to refine campaigns, contrasting this with tools like Clay that have a steep learning curve and little support.
moments.quote: And for us, we are, we're very sort of heavy on the human side ourselves. So every customer of ours has a customer success manager.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish's advice for founders with struggling outbound: pick 200 ideal customers, manually send hyper-personalized messages, learn what resonates, and only then automate the proven motion.
moments.quote: Yeah, I'd say if outbound isn't working for you and you've got a small sales team, go back to fundamentals, go back to basics.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

moments.title: Dalgleish reflects on selling a product to people it may partly replace, saying Perlon positions itself as an assist that removes manual drudgery and hopes teams grow rather than shrink.
moments.quote: I guess I've never been asked what it's like to sell a product into a group of people that you're effectively, in some ways, trying to replace.
moments.speaker: St John Dalgleish

move.text: Jay uses process mining. An agent scans ClickUp's full workspace history and proposes which processes to hand to agents. ClickUp plans to offer this to customers.
move.quote: you just have an agent go off for you and figure out what things you should be automating in the first place

numbers.text: Jay puts internal agents at roughly 10 to 1 against staff, up from 3 to 1. He gave no revenue or cost figures for the ROI.
numbers.quote: and say it's 3 to 1. I have to imagine it's closer to 10 to 1 at this point.

broke.text: Jay admits organisations are not ready for agents that work like executives. He expects adoption to trail frontier capability by a year to eighteen months.
broke.quote: There's many things that need to shift in the structure of organizations to be able to take on employees

advice.text: Map your daily work with a chat assistant and ask what it could automate. Then spend an hour with an agent designing one process.
advice.quote: for those specific processes, spend an hour and chat with an agent.

moments.title: Jay explains why he founded Codegen in late 2022: code is easy to verify, which keeps language models on the rails, and autocomplete scope could keep expanding from lines to whole codebases.
moments.quote: Sure. Yeah, there's a lot to unpack there. So Codegen started in late 2022, and at the time, the GPT-3 API had just opened up.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay describes Codegen's 'build me Netflix' vision: handing entire tasks to an AI that writes code, provisions infrastructure and even recruits, like level-5 self-driving for software.
moments.quote: I always thought about it as skating to where the puck is going. So instead of using the technology for what it was capable of at the time, trying to construct the next thing that we would be going towards as a society.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay explains why ClickUp was a better home for agents: its unified workspace avoids the data silos and Slack-style data walls that left Codegen agents unable to find organizational context.
moments.quote: And ClickUp had this incredible property, which was it had all of the apps that you care about in order to do a good job at a very wide variety of knowledge work in one place.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay reframes the agents-outnumber-employees claim as the latest step in automation, says the internal ratio is likely near 10 to 1, and argues the right metric is the share of work done autonomously by agents.
moments.quote: I mean, I see this as just the latest step in a long progression of increasing automation of knowledge work.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay lays out a three-step adoption hierarchy: autocomplete, then a synchronous sidebar chat, then asynchronous and parallel agents, with each step making the next easier to adopt.
moments.quote: I think there is a hierarchical progression of adoption of automation, and it follows something very similar to what we saw happen in the software engineering industry, which, you know, I'm a trained programmer.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Internal influencers publicly demonstrate agents in shared, multiplayer threads, so colleagues watching see the output and replicate it, creating a bottom-up virality mechanism.
moments.quote: In terms of driving adoption inside our internal workspace, you know, we have this massive ClickUp instance that's been spinning since 2017.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Top-down process mining: have an agent review your recent work and identify automatable processes and handoff friction, an approach ClickUp's CEO hacked together and ClickUp plans to institutionalize.
moments.quote: Top down though is also a very useful method that we've identified. And the idea is you just have an agent go off for you and figure out what things you should be automating in the first place.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: For first workflows, start with a sidebar agent for prioritization, research and drafting, then ask it to run recurring tasks, such as a 7 AM daily dossier, and let it help you climb the autonomy ladder.
moments.quote: So we have a sidebar in the ClickUp product, and I'm sure many other products have something similar where you click a button and this thing pops out where it's an agent who's sitting there and doing your work with you.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: ClickUp governs agents by treating them like users or contractors with granular permissions and requiring explicit human confirmation for destructive actions like deleting backlog tasks.
moments.quote: This is something we think about every day. It's the, you know, since the very foundation of our AI program.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay rejects the 'can an agent do the work' premise, invoking the lump of labor fallacy: automation expands the scope of ambition, so ClickUp is still hiring, with a higher bar for adaptable, agent-leveraging people.
moments.quote: I think there's this idea of the lump of labor fallacy, which is well known, goes back centuries where people always think there's only a certain amount of work.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay says non-technical rollouts mirrored software engineering's adoption pattern about two years later, while capability growth and eagerness to adopt agents, compared with the slow cloud transition, surprised him.
moments.quote: The unexpected, you know, I would say that for the majority, I would say that my experience of rolling out agents to knowledge workers who are largely non-technical, not all non-technical, but mostly people who are, you know, it's like accounting firms, marketing firms, PR firms, construction companies.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay predicts that within a year a single agent could act as executive, engineer and marketer in one, that organizations aren't prepared for this, and that adoption will trail frontier capability by one to one-and-a-half years.
moments.quote: Well, you know, I think that you could say for the type of agents that we are building today, how many years until people have mass adoption?
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay's one-week starting plan: chat with agents and plug in MCPs, then map your daily tasks with a chat client to find automatable ones, and spend an hour building one focused agentic process and refining it.
moments.quote: I think that the best way to familiarize yourself with AI capabilities is chatting with agents and just plugging in MCPs. And MCP is an integration to an external service.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

moments.title: Jay says people are stuck in catch-up mode despite a huge capabilities overhang and should ask what comes next; he expects near-term superintelligence that will crush any knowledge work and says he is still wrestling with the implications.
moments.quote: I think that there is this huge capabilities overhang already where agents are capable of doing things that, you know, you and I can't even fathom. They're solving frontier math questions.
moments.speaker: Jay Hack

move.text: Wouter moved skills tests to the top of the hiring funnel. AI interviews built by in-house scientists now replace first-round interviews.
move.quote: rather than doing a first-round interview, you can just send our AI interviews at first round.

numbers.text: TestGorilla launched in 2020 and has raised $80 million over three rounds. It has about 120 remote staff across 50 countries.
numbers.quote: We did 3 rounds of venture capital, raised $80 million, so 8-0 USD in total.

broke.text: Wouter admits they hired expensive, experienced sales staff before the sales-led motion was ready, and threw headcount at every problem. Money was wasted.
broke.quote: And I think we went way too aggressive at some point on the SLG.

advice.text: Do not run a vocabulary test. Wouter says to ask candidates for a workflow they built and what went wrong, not which tools they use.
advice.quote: give me an example of a workflow that you built and how did you do it? Did you bump into what went wrong?

moments.title: Wouter recounts how struggling to fairly and efficiently screen thousands of CVs at his remote rug social enterprise led him to copy-paste skills tests and then flip assessment to the top of the funnel, inspiring TestGorilla.
moments.quote: Yeah, the idea for TestGorilla was really born out of my own struggles with hiring, struggles with hiring as an entrepreneur. So I've been an entrepreneur for basically my whole life.
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter explains that AI hasn't changed TestGorilla's mission but made it more urgent, since the old-fashioned CV is worthless when every candidate has a perfect AI-made CV.
moments.quote: But it's mostly creating— I think it made our mission actually more urgent, right? If you look at our biggest competitor, like the old-fashioned CV, it's just worthless these days, right?
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter lays out TestGorilla's five-pillar AI fluency framework (applied use, learning agility, systems thinking, responsible use, human-AI collaboration) and warns that asking which tools someone uses becomes a vocabulary test.
moments.quote: Yeah, great question. And I think one that a lot of customers ask us as well. And the main topic is, how do I test for AI fluency?
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter warns white-collar workers with long careers to learn AI tools, and describes moving internally from the carrot of celebrating AI to the stick of making it part of performance reviews.
moments.quote: I think in white-collar roles, if you still have a long career ahead of you, you better, yeah, get on the bandwagon, right?
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter shares State of AI Fluency findings: 95% of hiring leaders call AI fluency a requirement, but ~60% have already mis-hired and ~40% define the bar as knowing what tools exist.
moments.quote: Yeah, yeah, we just launched this report. Yeah, but I think we interviewed over 3,000 hiring managers and recruiters and founders.
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter admits TestGorilla hired people who talked positively about AI but had crammed vocabulary, then tightened its process using its own assessments, and describes how AI-first work has made senior leaders hands-on builders again.
moments.quote: Yeah, 100%. It's changed completely how we hire and how we work. On the hiring side, yeah, we're lucky to have all these scientists at our company, right, who built that AI fluency framework.
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter reflects that the main thing capital buys is time and room for mistakes, but a big raise tempts you to throw an FTE at every problem, which he wouldn't do again.
moments.quote: Yeah, nice question. Yeah, it was a very big raise for how small we were at the time, right? I think the main thing capital buys you as an entrepreneur is time, and that, that's incredibly valuable.
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter says his CEO anxiety is how fast tiny startups can build with AI compared to an established scale-up, though adopting AI and changing ways of working can let larger teams move faster.
moments.quote: Yeah, I think the one thing that gives me a bit of anxiety is just the speed at which very small teams, small scale-up startups, sorry, can build things. Right.
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Years of experience is a far weaker signal now, while demonstrated proof of what you can do and human skills like judgment survive in the AI era.
moments.quote: Yeah, I think traditional signals, like just years of experience, work experience, right? One of the signals that most recruiters, traditional recruiters, would look at most is way less relevant, right?
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

moments.title: Wouter tells how skills-based hiring surfaced a Venezuelan medical doctor with no professional SEO history who ranked number one on the SEO assessment, a gem a CV filter would have rejected instantly.
moments.quote: Yeah, so of course we come from assessments, right? That's where we started. And I think a lot of people ask us about how to screen people out, right?
moments.speaker: Wouter Durville

move.text: Kai is staying Europe-only and widening Enginy from a scrappy data aggregator into an end-to-end AI sales CRM, built on multilingual first-party data.
move.quote: Let's build a category-defining software sales CRM as a category that dominates Europe.

numbers.text: Enginy passed €6M ARR in 24 months with 60 to 65 staff. Kai expects 10M ARR by year end and is hiring 30-plus in product and engineering.
numbers.quote: We managed to grow to, to grow to, to €6 million ARR with 60, 65 people in our team.

broke.text: Kai admits forecasting and budgeting were neglected early, and the scrappy aggregator that won the first customers will not reach $100M.
broke.quote: some of these things were some things that we didn't pay attention before and we start to pay attention now

advice.text: Kai tells founders to pay staff for LinkedIn milestones and gamify posting, such as $1K and a day off at 10K followers.
advice.quote: Put incentives and some game around it to enable and activate this motion in the short run.

moments.title: Brandt argues funding doesn't imply efficiency; Spain's tough VC climate forced Enginy into a profitable-growth, AI-leveraged mindset that let it compete with 10x better-funded rivals.
moments.quote: Well, I think, like, funding doesn't necessarily imply efficiency, right? Indeed, the more funded you are, the less efficient your growth is. And founders tend to underestimate it, right?
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Being born post-AI let Enginy reinvent functions, processes and team structures from scratch, reaching $6M ARR with 60-65 people.
moments.quote: And that helped a lot, especially being post-AI. We had an advantage amongst other players that were born before because we could reinvent from scratch many functions, many processes, the way we run teams, which is something you cannot do once you start building and operating a team that is pre-AI.
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Brandt explains why Enginy entered a crowded market: sales stacks of 6-10 point tools are inefficient, and the future seller will work through a single AI system of action.
moments.quote: When you look at the category, there's many, let's say, point solutions, as I named them. That focus on some part of the, let's say, end-to-end sales process or the GTM motion.
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Enginy entered as a scrappy data aggregator, and Brandt argues that as AI commoditizes software development, distribution plays a really, really, really big role.
moments.quote: However, this is the vision, right? The way we entered the market was being this kind of scrappy tool that allowed you to pull data across different sources. ...
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Brandt lists Barcelona's advantages: quality of life, dense and affordable engineering talent, a growing startup ecosystem and an appealing city for international hiring.
moments.quote: The beauty of Barcelona is I see many verticals in which, you know, some sort of arguments why I built from here. One of it is the personal one. ...
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Enginy's growth was mostly a GTM advantage: using its own product for high-intent outbound, intense cold calling and organic LinkedIn content.
moments.quote: Yeah, I think I would say it's mostly a GTM advantage. ... So our main growth channel has been outbound for us, using and leveraging our own technology and our own product to do high-intent targeting, automated outreach, You know, we were quite intense in cold calling.
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Telling employees to post failed until Enginy added cash bonuses, vacation days, a leaderboard and a points-based game tied to LinkedIn milestones.
moments.quote: Yeah, so we started like just telling the team go post on LinkedIn, right? And of course that doesn't work if it's not aligned to their incentives. ...
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Incentives only kickstart posting; long term, sellers keep posting because audience and trust make outbound easier.
moments.quote: I think the combination of these 2 will make them to post. And at the long run, what keeps them posting is not this. ...
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Brandt describes using Claude and MCP so non-technical staff can run GTM workflows in plain language, from list building and segmentation to dashboards.
moments.quote: Yeah, so I think what Claude has made is the ability of everyone in your team who is not necessarily tech savvy to be able to do complex GTM workflows using plain language.
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: The claim that AI can replace SDRs is obviously not true, but properly prompted AI combines outreach volume with personalization when ICP, intent signals and messaging are matched.
moments.quote: It's probably you've seen 11x and some companies like that that sold the promise of, you know, AI is your SDR. ... That is obviously not true, right?
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Brandt says companies shouldn't rebuild all SaaS (the lettuce analogy), but should build custom tools like dashboards or invoice follow-ups where standard software doesn't fit.
moments.quote: Yeah, I mean, we, we didn't build lots of tools, to be honest. ... we're not growing our own lettuces, even if it would be cheaper than going to a supermarket, right?
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: What takes a company from 0 to $3M ARR won't take it to $100M: leadership, processes, forecasting and a bigger product narrative are needed, with 30+ product and engineering hires planned.
moments.quote: I think we cracked the 0 to 1 in some ways. But, you know, what takes you from 0 to 1 million, 2 million, 3 million of ARR is not what will take you to 100.
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Initially Brandt just wanted a hacky, scrappy product to win early clients; the long-term end-to-end vision only came after rapid growth and product-market fit.
moments.quote: At that time, it's mostly how can I find something hacky and scrappy enough so that not a lot of people have it in the market and people will like to buy it ...
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Brandt argues models, third-party data and even product features will be commoditized, so first-party sales data is the durable moat.
moments.quote: When I think about in the era of AI, 5 years from now, the company that will win the market is the one that models are going to come— well, they are already a commodity.
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: To build the first-party data moat Enginy needs to be the everyday sales platform (CRM, dialer) and capture multilingual European sales data that US peers lack.
moments.quote: One, we need to have a sales CRM. We need to have a dialer. ... We need to be the everyday platform for anyone in sales, SDRs, AEs, whoever, right?
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

moments.title: Brandt shares the habit changes (quitting smoking and drinking, sport, meditation, 8-10 hours of sleep) that sustain his decision quality, noting most founders optimize for everything but their sleep.
moments.quote: I mean, I, I, I, I used to smoke. I quit smoking. Yeah. I quit drinking. ... whenever I don't do sports because I'm traveling, I truly think I take worse decisions than when I do them, right?
moments.speaker: Kai Brandt

move.text: Aleks chose to build horizontally from day one, against Lean Startup advice, betting that billing can only be fixed end to end.
move.quote: the only way for us to solve this properly is if we try to solve it as horizontally as possible at the time

numbers.text: Aleks cites research that top AI B2B SaaS companies change pricing 3.6 times a year, roughly every 90 to 100 days.
numbers.quote: top 500 AI B2B SaaS companies have changed pricing on average 3.6 times a year, which averages like 90 to 100 days.

broke.text: Trust remains the number one objection, followed by whether a young company like Alguna will still be around.
broke.quote: building trust from the get-go has always been number one objection, followed by, are you going to be around?

advice.text: Aleks says pricing is a new product line. Give it a dedicated owner and engineering team, not an ad hoc 12-month project.
advice.quote: every company now has a new product line that they're not aware of, which is pricing.

moments.title: Aleks explains Alguna's origin: after seeing sales flexibility and billing control work at Dojo, he hit the pain of integrating 5-6 tools to launch new pricing at a payment-orchestration company.
moments.quote: I wish it was just one night. It was a few months of, and years of like painfully experiencing the same problem all over again in any pretty much B2B company that I've been part of.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: A billing prototype is easy in isolation, but the real moat is a foundation ensuring "whatever sales quotes, billing can bill" across discounts, credits, usage and hybrid terms, which enables rapid module-building later.
moments.quote: If it's done in isolation with a specific use case that you want to achieve, it is possible to do in that one Sunday morning. But the problem comes to scale and flexibility over time.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks cites research that top AI B2B SaaS companies change pricing about 3.6 times a year (~90 days), caveats that the average is skewed by firms like Anthropic, and warns that margin erosion from 80% to 50% will force change.
moments.quote: Yeah, it's from research from Growth Unhinged from Kyle Poyer. Okay. Yeah, that's the average that they have come up with. Our thesis was changing every 90 days from like our own kind of research in that way.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Pricing is nominally owned by one person but needs input from finance, engineering, product, sales and rev ops, so "no one owns it. Everybody wants to have an input," and customers suffer through inconsistent pricing.
