moments.quote: Historically, 6 months of hiring some pricing consulting team coming in, seeing your usage, seeing the benchmarks, doing all the research and seeing what people are willing to pay and how they would pay that, which in B2C works really well at scale.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Pricing consultants still help, but implementation is the bottleneck: a public company made 8 pricing changes in 15 years, and companies shouldn't wait 6 months to bill a new pricing SKU.
moments.quote: Yeah. And I think they're still They still need to be involved in the process because they can save you a lot of time and trouble by having that kind of experience.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Pricing is as much art as science; since a small share of users drive most usage and switching straight to usage-based cuts reportable revenue, companies should adopt hybrid models with upfront usage plus overages.
moments.quote: Pricing is as much science as art, or as much art as science. And it's a two-way street between somebody who is buying and person who is selling.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks lays out levers for making usage pricing predictable: shared allowances, threshold alerts with customer success offering prepaid bulk discounts, surge protection, tiers, min/max spends, credits, ramps and phases.
moments.quote: One of these was setting up that kind of like a layer of allowance to use either per actual seats, a pair of seats, or Like, actually just as like a company shared pool of usage.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks argues the claim that everything will move to outcome-based pricing is wrong: it works for customer support like Fin and Sierra where success is objective, but boards' ARR expectations and unclear outcomes mean no overnight flip.
moments.quote: Wrong. It's always a little bit more on the kind of like case-by-case basis.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks calls the outcome-pricing hype an echo chamber; even if inevitable, taped-together billing tools make pricing changes hard, requiring either a costly rip-and-replace or gradual point-solution upgrades.
moments.quote: It's a little bit of an echo chamber, I would say. Especially if my algorithm is trained to look for pricing, pricing, pricing, and different billing and monetization flows.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks describes CFOs and CROs reconciling spreadsheets on Friday and Saturday nights, and defines the sales-finance chasm between the contract sales signed and what finance invoices, which Alguna bridges with a single source of truth.
moments.quote: We made from day one, we tried to really approach this from a first principle.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Alguna won its first 10 customers organically through trust and design partnerships with forward-deployed-style engineers, deliberately spreading wide rather than following Lean Startup, and built reputation by showing up when things go wrong.
moments.quote: And first 10 customers was really actually organic. We didn't leverage, not that I ever had a big network of, like, I'm a first-time founder as well as my co-founder.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Alguna said it would never build payments, invoicing or dunning, but its first customer needed them, expanding the product to about 30% more scope and becoming a key advantage by letting finance teams close the month in minutes.
moments.quote: We always said the background, both my co-founder and I are in payments. And we said we will never touch payments and we will never touch invoicing and dunning and retries and all that.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: To earn trust from buyers replacing critical billing infrastructure, Alguna involves technical teams early, uses the customer's data by the second call, and asks prospects to push the platform's limits to find the missing 10% before implementation.
moments.quote: We try to involve technical teams from early on. So our product engineers are called product engineers because they build the product, but they also support our customers on their journey.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks says prioritization is his hardest challenge; he uses the pipeline to decide where to invest while resisting shiny-object features and customers.
moments.quote: Prioritization is number one. Being able to know where resources need to go, where you need to invest more and where you need to invest less.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks predicts per-seat pricing survives in some form because of predictability needs, as pure usage models require investor patience and a long-term view that most seed-to-Series B founders can't afford given ARR benchmarks.
moments.quote: I think some shape or form will stay forever because the predictability would be needed. I think, and this is going to sound controversial, so let's see how this is going to go.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: The companies most exposed by AI are those with multiple stitched-together tools across CPQ, invoicing, billing, payments and collections, or spreadsheets; those with usage components and engineering involved in pricing are ahead.
moments.quote: The most exposed one, the ones that have multiple tools that are stitched together and most of the time don't work well when they're stitched together, from like CPQ, document design, invoicing, billing, payments, collections.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

moments.title: Aleks argues every company now has a new product line, pricing, which needs a dedicated owner, engineering team and stakeholders, with continuous margin-aware iteration instead of an ad hoc 12-month project.
moments.quote: I would say It would be that every company now has a new product line that they're not aware of, which is pricing.
moments.speaker: Aleks Đekić

move.text: Light dropped its OCR partner and offshore human checkers for bills. Two agents now parse each bill and must agree before it reaches the user.
move.quote: now we have basically 2 agents, one that does a first OCR and a second one that double checks everything the first agent's doing

numbers.text: Light runs on about 100 employees with a single person in finance. Jonathan says every BDR is above 2x quota.
numbers.quote: So we're a company of like 100 employees. We have one person in finance running the whole show.

broke.text: Jonathan assumed customers would find it easy to tell agents what to do. Many did not, and needed training to manage agents well.
broke.quote: I thought that would be really easy to describe what you wanted the agents to do and have them do that.

advice.text: Start agents on one simple task and add complexity once they follow instructions. Do not dump 20 pages of old operating principles on them.
advice.quote: you want to sort of maybe start out quite simple and make sure that it does that

moments.title: Sanders describes Light as an intelligent finance platform for globally scaling companies, positioned between Xero/QuickBooks and legacy ERPs, consolidating payments, approvals, and financial statements.
moments.quote: Yes. So Light is the finance platform. We're building this intelligent finance platform for companies that want to scale globally.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: After migrating to Oracle ERP at both Pleo and Juny, Sanders saw that legacy systems take a year to implement, deliver little value and need point solutions, inspiring Light's unified accounting and payments approach.
moments.quote: I saw the journey twice where we migrated to an Oracle ERP, first at Pleo and then at Juny. And both of those companies were of course created in smaller countries.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Legacy ERPs span CRM to HR to accounting with thousands of tables, confusing agents (Copilot in ERP reportedly doesn't work), while Light is purpose-built around finance and AI from day one.
moments.quote: So. We, when we started Light, we had this view that we want this platform that can handle both the accounting side and the payment side. And Light is the only sort of company that does that.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Sanders argues ERPs are less sticky than assumed because Light uses AI to clean, validate, map and migrate data, and that AI lowers switching costs even as bespoke agents can raise them.
moments.quote: Yeah, exactly. You're on zero until it breaks and it sort of breaks at the moment you start to be like multinational and that's when you start to have all of these issues.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Beyond speed, AI can add control and accuracy: agents can perform audit-like checks previously uneconomical, with agents checking other agents' work and applying multiple accounting standards with sourcing.
moments.quote: Well, I think for finance teams, you want speed, you want control, and you want accuracy.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Light's bill-processing evolved from OCR to OCR plus offshore human verification, which still had errors, to a two-agent setup where one processes and the other checks, flagging disagreements, and it proved more accurate than humans.
moments.quote: Yeah, we aim for better than human. So I'll give you one example. We, the very first sort of use case of agent was that we had this module in the platform that allowed you to That it allows you to forward bills into the platform.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Sanders argues automation doesn't eliminate finance jobs but frees capacity for controls like sanctions and VAT checks, illustrated by a gambling company using agents to monitor regulator payments and filing dates.
moments.quote: And I think when it comes to data entry and classifications, such as making sure that it comes in different labels, once you have enough context that you've given into a system, the system will very shortly after a couple of weeks outperform what you would normally have.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Adopting Light requires learning to manage agents; controllers and AP/AR staff translate each company's bespoke context and approval culture into agent setups, while Light's memory builds knowledge about the business.
moments.quote: You need to manage agents, but that is spot on. You need to manage agents. So that is part of the transition is to make sure that you're able to manage agents.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Asked about the most wrong beliefs on AI in finance, Sanders names fear of job loss and fear of losing control, arguing proper environments allow more controls and audit assertions than before.
moments.quote: I think the most wrong thing, number one, It is fear that it's going to lead to job loss. That's the— it's not quite— you don't hear it as much, but it's always sort of unspoken.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Sanders didn't anticipate that managing agents is a skill; his advice is to start with simple tasks, confirm the agent follows instructions, then layer in complexity rather than dumping in decade-old operating documents.
moments.quote: They needed more, more, they, me specifically, I did not anticipate that you need, it's a certain skill set and it's a certain A little, a slightly different way of working when you're managing agents than when you are basically not managing any other employees.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Light runs hackathons with partners like Lovable, JP Morgan, Deloitte and McKinsey where finance professionals build solutions to their own workflow problems, some using them the next day, discovering AI is easier than expected.
moments.quote: And I think the best one is probably in the go-to-market side where we are, you know, we were thinking, how can we give people a little bit of like a taste for what AI is?
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Sanders argues legacy software left finance teams dependent on IT consultants for every change, and AI lets finance professionals change software themselves, since software should serve the power user, not foster an industry of third parties.
moments.quote: But I think there has been a little bit of apprehension about it. And I think now in the last year, year and a half, we've come a long way in hopefully educating the market in our segment about what is actually possible.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Light builds trust in AI on the general ledger via an immutable ledger with a permanent audit trail, scoped and configurable agent guardrails, uploadable board-approved GAAP/IFRS policies, and by judging overall system accuracy against the real human-plus-software alternative.
moments.quote: We made a lot of choices from day one in how to build the general ledger. So in Light is one of the few general ledgers globally that is immutable.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

moments.title: Sanders says the hardest parts of scaling are that AI's potential is far from fully tapped, requiring radical UX innovation, and hiring people who understand enterprise context yet think from first principles on a new canvas.
moments.quote: I mean, AI is is difficult. AI is, is truly difficult. and I'm saying that not because we're not sort of an AI native or first or whatever you want to claim to be company.
moments.speaker: Jonathan Sanders

move.text: Semir chose not to hire or use agencies. He rebuilt the website in code with Claude and automated blogs, the help centre and operational alerts.
move.quote: Because I was at the point of, should we hire somebody? Should I get an agency to help me on the marketing side?

numbers.text: Semir estimates agencies would have cost $20,000 to $40,000. AI subscriptions cost a few hundred dollars. Self-serve sign-ups now arrive at least a handful a week.
numbers.quote: $20K, $30K, $40K spent that we would have had to invest. And that was just a few hundred dollars on AI subscriptions.

broke.text: Semir admits the AI-written help centre may be only 90% correct. He barely reads the automated blog posts and has no hard data on conversion yet.
broke.quote: And maybe it's 90% correct. Maybe there's some false assumptions in here.

advice.text: Semir tells founders to ask of every task whether AI can do it. He suggests automating the work around revenue and core product first.
advice.quote: I would just really encourage people, can this be done with AI? It's much farther along than many might think.

moments.title: Semir explains that Claude Opus and Codex ended his debates about hiring or buying agency help, so two people can punch above their weight in sales tech.
moments.quote: And in the last 6 months, especially with this Claude Opus coming out and Codex, it's been a real game changer in how more effectively and more productively we can run with just 2 people still.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir's core advice for 2026 founders is to make 'Can this be done with AI?' a reflex and to ship at the speed of thinking.
moments.quote: Yeah, I mean, it's, I mean, 2026, probably every founder has excitement and anxiety emotions at the same exact moment in time because AI is getting more powerful.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir replaced a clunky HubSpot CMS site with a code-based site built via Cursor, GitHub and Vercel, so he can now prompt the website instead of using a CMS.
moments.quote: So what AI really has helped me do since February was like kind of our website. It was kind of this thing we had, like, you know, just like a landing page.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir avoids generic AI slop by having AI mine his CRM, Gmail and Granola call transcripts to write anonymized, customer-informed content for segments like life sciences.
moments.quote: The way that you kind of get a bit around that AI slop objection sometimes, because yes, if you just say, hey, create me 50 blog posts on sales, it'll be a bit AI sloppish.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir describes his blog pipeline: Outrank for automatic posts, plus a Claude content plan built from recent meetings, emails and competitors that he reviews and that is then produced automatically with only light skimming.
moments.quote: it's more like that. And I don't need to read it as much. There's a, there's a couple of things that are running. So one thing, another tool that I use is called Outrank.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Instead of complaints about AI-written content, a salesperson thanked Semir for an AI-generated PDF sales-methodology template after losing their old one.
moments.quote: I've had I've had people actually reach out for the opposite. They said that this was a very useful post.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Since the website rebuild, demo bookings have risen and a handful of self-service sign-ups arrive weekly, many discovering Salesmotion through ChatGPT and Claude.
moments.quote: I think our demo books have gone up quite a bit since then. I think we had like inbound through like Google a little bit, mostly through LinkedIn because I post on LinkedIn a lot.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: As a scrappy bootstrapper, Semir had Claude set up self-hosted Plausible analytics on a $2-a-month Hetzner server in about two hours, saving roughly $100 a year.
moments.quote: I mean, Google Analytics is very complicated. Plausible is like an open source, like semi-open source thing, and you can pay for it like $100 a year.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: A long-delayed knowledge base got built when Semir had Claude generate help-center articles from his emails, calls, resolved tickets and product code instead of paying for Intercom.
moments.quote: So then I think as a founder, you're always like, oh, okay, we need more traffic, top of funnel, we need to build the product.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: The AI-written knowledge base is maybe 90% correct with no complaints yet, and it frees founder time for pipeline by tackling tasks that would otherwise never get done.
moments.quote: So I have not written any of these articles and it will have everything in here, including nice tables. It breaks it and has access to the code as well of our actual tools.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir runs Slack alerts, CRM syncs, meeting briefs and a weekly traffic analysis from one operations repo on Vercel, keeping his time for customers and strategy because everything else gets automated.
moments.quote: So essentially what we've done is we've done a lot of stuff in our Salesmotion operations repo, if you want, where we talk about Slack notifications that go out for all sorts of things like, hey, there's website visitors, abandoned carts.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir asks 'can I automate this?' the second time a task recurs, but weighs buy versus build and skips rebuilding tools like Granola, while building notifications, CRM updates and late-payment locks himself.
moments.quote: Yeah, I mean, the question definitely comes up the second time around if I then get to automate it because sometimes I'm like, let's just do it.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir prototypes product ideas himself in a GitHub branch of the real app so his CTO receives a visual, clickable version and can focus on production reliability rather than interpreting verbal descriptions.
moments.quote: And the beautiful thing is we can now really iterate fast on the product as well because we talk a lot about the business side and the marketing and the sales side of everything we're doing.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir says an idea can reach production almost immediately in low-risk domains like sales tech, notes that regulated fields like fintech need guardrails, and urges founders to start with adjacent tasks such as marketing, help centers and notifications.
moments.quote: Like what I said, you can really ship at the speed of thinking almost.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Asked about agent-led sales, Semir warns against the LinkedIn echo chamber and argues that AI-driven research and tailored emails, meetings and decks are now baseline buyer expectations.
moments.quote: Yeah, I think it's hard to say still. I mean, so much is changing all the time, and I think it's always important to kind of remember to not fall into the kind of the, what's it called, like the echo chamber of LinkedIn and your founder friends who are all at the bleeding edge.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: With email and LinkedIn saturated by AI spam and polished AI-startup sites easy to fake, Semir says personal connection, case studies and in-person meetings become more valuable in bigger deals.
moments.quote: But I do think as well, I think on one hand, it's so much easier. You get a lot of these AI spam cannons these days. Email is saturated, LinkedIn is saturated.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir expects a breaking point but says AI saved $20–40K of agency spend for a few hundred dollars of subscriptions, so he'll automate everything non-core first before hiring in sales, customer success or engineering.
moments.quote: I mean, I think like— I mean, a little bit like you as well, like you want to try to see how far you can go.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir admits he doesn't know the moat, but points to hard data work, customer happiness and bootstrapped agility, noting that VC-backed competitors were acquired or shut down while Salesmotion kept going.
moments.quote: Yeah, I think it's that question that every founder is, that's the anxiety part, I think, of that excitement and anxiety between about 30 minutes now about the excitement piece.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

moments.title: Semir warns that cheap all-inclusive AI subscriptions may give way to credit-based pricing and that thinking consciously about model choice, prompts and efficiency from the start will prevent a cost wake-up call.
moments.quote: And with the efficiency in mind, one other thing I'm seeing now at least is with these IPOs coming closer of the big companies is it might not stay so cheap forever.
moments.speaker: Semir Jahic

move.text: Adam renamed Glyphic to Airspeed after customers pushed the product from insight towards execution, using an agency for the name and vibe-coding the website.
move.quote: move more from that kind of intelligence language type of name to something that has some significance around speed, around motion

numbers.text: Adam closed the Series A early in the year and very quickly doubled the team, which now stands at 35 people.
numbers.quote: we closed it early in the year. We announced it just recently. It was kind of very very quickly double the size of the team.

broke.text: Product token spend is rising as agents grow more capable, eating into margins while pricing stays mostly seat-based. Adam expects to move to consumption pricing.
broke.quote: especially kind of as we make the agents more flexible, being able to do more things, which definitely kind of eats into our margins

advice.text: Adam tells founders to run regular AI hackathons, as customer Firmat Commerce does, and push reluctant staff to automate their own workflows.
advice.quote: everyone is tasked to kind of explore AI tools for their own workflows and see how far they can push the automations

moments.title: Adam explains he and Devang left DeepMind in 2022 to build with users and iterate quickly as AI moved from understanding sentences to whole conversations.
moments.quote: Yeah, no, good question. And we get this one often, as you can imagine. Well, so Devang and I, we met at DeepMind.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Sales and customer conversations are unique, unstructured organizational data that should drive company strategy, unlike commoditized public data.
moments.quote: Yeah, so there's a gap, and there's also a long-term kind of vision behind the company.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam explains the Glyphic-to-Airspeed rebrand: the old name was hard to pronounce, and the product had shifted from intelligence toward execution and speed.
moments.quote: Yeah, 2 things really that led us to the rebrand. I think one thing is people didn't know how to pronounce it. And I think one, you're in a company— Incorrect, actually.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Two decades of GTM tools collected data and built dashboards, but none closed the gap between knowing what to do and doing it, which is what moves revenue and pipeline.
moments.quote: Yeah, so kind of when you look at the go-to-market tech stack over the last 20, 25 years, it's been mostly systems that collect data, aggregate data.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: AI-native means agents can do anything a human can in the system and AI makes decisions rather than running hardcoded sequences.
moments.quote: Yeah, so I mean, AI washing, agent washing, there's a lot of that kind of happening right now, especially kind of as the legacy tools kind of try to show that they're doing something in the AI space.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Airspeed is mostly seat-based today but is looking at consumption or hybrid pricing, and says rising token costs from more flexible agents make consumption pricing the likely direction.
moments.quote: We're still mostly seat-based. We're innovating on kind of several different directions and we didn't want to innovate both on how do we deliver the value and the pricing. But we're looking at consumption pricing as well.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: The claim that AI replaces salespeople misunderstands the role: AI removes CRM updates, research and drafting while humans keep engaging prospects and understanding pain points in upper mid-market and enterprise sales.
moments.quote: I would say Most really that AI is kind of replacing salespeople. We've heard something similar in, for example, software engineering.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam recommends re-engaging quiet prospects weekly because the underlying problem that prompted the conversation likely persists even if priorities shifted.
moments.quote: I'm just curious, I guess, from a personal level. So let's say a prospective customer has gone quiet. How often would you recommend that you reengage, that you continue to try this person if they're not responding?
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Moving from research to product, Adam learned that reliability across varied real-world use cases matters more than peak performance, so new frontier models must be evaluated before replacing existing ones.
moments.quote: Yeah, I mean, there's a lot of things going from a more research environment to a product environment. I think one of the big ones is around performance and kind of how do people evaluate performance?
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: As a first-time CEO, Adam most enjoys building and talking to users, while the hardest part is letting go of work he's mastered to push the company's frontier.
moments.quote: Yeah, so I mean, I'm an engineer researcher by background, so I really like building products, talking to users, seeing the value that we bring. I think that's the most satisfying part of the job.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Early users unexpectedly shared Airspeed outputs company-wide, and customers pushed the product into sales coaching and one-to-one support.
moments.quote: What surprised us is when we rolled out the product to our customers and to our users the first time, they started sharing the outputs and screenshots internally.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Selling a sales tool to sales teams invites scrutiny: early 2023 LLMs confused buyer and seller, so Airspeed aims to model consultative selling and takes buyers on an AI journey matched to their comfort level.
moments.quote: Yeah, definitely. So, yeah, I mean, selling a sales tool to sales teams, it comes with a lot of kind of funny situations.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: After the Series A, Adam's hardest challenges were doubling the team to create clear owners, differentiating positioning in a crowded GTM market, and countering build-versus-buy thinking with maintenance costs.
moments.quote: Yeah. So, well, I think one thing that was super difficult was around scaling the team. So it was a big focus right after we fundraised. We announced, yeah, we closed it early in the year.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Alex describes building replacements for tools to about 40% completion before the maintenance burden hits, and Adam predicts a balance of internal builds with dedicated software for core GTM tasks.
moments.quote: That's the sad thing that gets me because I probably, like many, I'm super excited about the capabilities of what I can finally build now, right? I couldn't last year or a few years ago.
moments.speaker: Alex Theuma

moments.title: Adam separates internal token use, which is not yet a problem and which he pushes every function to increase, from product token spend, which is rising with flexible agents and pushing Airspeed toward consumption pricing.
moments.quote: So I think there's 2 different use cases. One is tokens used to do work internally.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam explains GTM skepticism: fully-replace-salespeople claims are nonsense, and GTM is harder for AI than coding because context spans thousands of daily conversations rather than one codebase.
moments.quote: No. So, I mean, there's definitely areas within GTM that are amenable to very quick kind of AI wins.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam qualifies that AI will automate simple transactional sales end to end, but complex upper mid-market and enterprise deals with many stakeholders and unclear buyer problems still need humans.
moments.quote: So yeah, let me maybe qualify that. I think on the lower end, kind of simple transactional sales, definitely AI will kind of automate that end to end.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam says AI cold calls will annoy people and saturate, but AI voice or video bots that engage inbound website buyers instead of making them wait for an AE or SDR make sense.
moments.quote: I mean, I did receive calls from AI. It's Yeah, I mean, I would engage just to kind of play with it, but at the same time, I don't think this is the best use case because I think you're just going to annoy people.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: The number of GTM tools won't shrink to one or two, but the user experience will collapse into one orchestration layer that owns some tasks and delegates others to integrated tools.
moments.quote: I don't think it's going to be one or two, but I think the experience will collapse.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam advises teams to run regular one-to-two-day AI hackathons like customer Firmat Commerce, with leads creating space, and pressure where needed, for everyone to automate their own workflows.
moments.quote: Well, Yeah, I mean, if they're running it in the traditional way, there's so much that they can do.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam says AI raises expected output per employee rather than reducing work: Airspeed still needs owners per function, and like Excel in the 1970s, faster tools mean more gets done, not a shorter workday.
moments.quote: Yeah, well, yeah, I mean, we will still need people. And so we needed to hire just so that we've got that ownership and owners of the different functions. Funnily enough, we also mostly— well, actually not true.
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

moments.title: Adam describes Airspeed's longer-term vision of programmable companies: a single space encoding company knowledge and workflows that humans and agents can use and keep improving, starting with GTM data.
moments.quote: So I think I actually didn't cover that at the beginning, but kind of the way I think about Airspeed, is how can we make the whole company run more efficiently?
moments.speaker: Adam Liska

move.text: Des and Eoin renamed the company Fin, keeping Intercom only as the help desk name, so the AI agent is judged against new AI companies.
move.quote: That's why we changed our email address, our domain, our blog, everything. It's all Fin.

numbers.text: Fin is already way over $100 million in revenue and resolves over 70% of queries. Engineering productivity tripled after going all in on Claude.
numbers.quote: Fin is growing faster than anything we've ever seen. And it's already a very substantial business too, way over $100 million in revenue.

broke.text: Per-resolution pricing undercharges. If Fin answers six of seven questions and then hands over to a human, the business pays nothing for that conversation.
broke.quote: So Fin could have done a phenomenal amount of work. It could have saved hours.

advice.text: Des tells founders to beware of cope. Drop the nostalgia and ask what you would build in your space if starting today.
advice.quote: If you were building a company in your space today, what would you build? What would it look like?

moments.title: Des explains Intercom's founding insight: subscription businesses needed loyalty and relationships, which require conversation, and the internet had no good way to do customer communication.
moments.quote: The original insight was every business was becoming a kind of an internet SaaS business, and there was no good way to do customer communication, full stop. You couldn't send messages to your customers.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des recalls an early user's excited monologue on a Skype call about talking to customers all day, which told him Intercom had hit product-market fit.
moments.quote: I think the thing that probably caught me off guard, I realized after me and Eoin had a conversation with one of our early users, and he just, as soon as the Skype call connected, that's how old it was, it was a Skype call.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des explains why Fin was always built as a separate identity from Intercom: to get a fresh look from the industry, sit alongside new AI companies, and work on other platforms like Salesforce and Zendesk.
moments.quote: Well, there's 2 separate things there. I think we always built Fin as a separate identity and as a separate named different thing to Intercom because we needed, at the very least, we needed the industry to kind of give us a fresh look.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des argues that legacy brand recognition can be a counterweight, using Workday building a payroll app as an example, and explains why retiring Intercom puts the onus on Fin to build its own brand equity.
moments.quote: I think people massively underestimate the degree to which their legacy can hold them back. And the way in which they underestimate is twofold. They don't realize how much just being known isn't always useful.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des says the first test of AI-native is whether the AI actually works, covering reliability, hallucination and escalation, then how Fin goes full stack with its Apex post-trained model and about 27 connected systems.
moments.quote: The biggest test initially is just, does the AI actually work? And it sounds silly to say that, but there's so many AI products out there that aren't performing at the level that they need to.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des predicts most SaaS products will converge on a simple text-box interaction model, with dashboards for recurring queries and creative tools like Photoshop and Ableton as exceptions.
moments.quote: I mean, at some point you realize those bells and whistles are really just bells and whistles. Like I think the future, like, I started a bit of a controversy on Twitter over this topic.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des argues that cheaper code and AI-native UI remove the two constraints that kept products small, so software will merge and converge across product boundaries.
moments.quote: Or at the very least, we're going to head for this era of what I would call the merge and converge.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des advises legacy SaaS founders to 'beware of cope' and evaluate their business coldly by asking what they would build today, and what they'd actually keep.
moments.quote: I guess beware of cope. It's useful to get a good distance from your company and to drop some of the nostalgia and fondness that you have for the way things were and evaluate things from a cold perspective.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des says Fin's teams are getting smaller, with merged EM/PM/engineer roles and tripled productivity from going all in on Claude Code.
moments.quote: I think it'll be leaner relative to the footprint of software and like the product categories that we want to play in. Definitely, yes. Already we see this in that the team sizes are smaller.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des defines a Fin resolution as an answer the user acknowledges or doesn't follow up on within 24 hours, and admits per-resolution pricing means Fin earns nothing when it does lots of work but hands over to a human.
moments.quote: The definition is basically pretty much exactly what we'd use for a human, which is like Fin gives an answer and the user can either directly or indirectly acknowledge that answer, or they can just go away.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des contrasts Intercom's historic Jobs-to-Be-Done, customer-first product process with the AI era, where customers can't specify what's possible and teams must start with the technology.
moments.quote: Well, historically, the way we built software in Intercom was we'd pick a certain job to be done, which would have been evidenced by a product manager through scores of product interviews.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des explains that during rapid technological change you must first establish what is doable, performant and reliable, using the example of inferring help docs from source code, and only then find the problems it solves.
moments.quote: So you really, like, the technology is changing too fast for our customers to be experts in anything other than the problems that they have.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des says brand is not the moat in AI right now: brand gets Fin into the consideration set, but performance in a bake-off is what wins the contract.
moments.quote: I don't think it is right now. I think right now performance is probably still the thing that like most of our larger customers, and we have like customers who like, you know, pay us for like millions of resolutions a year, say, right?
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des describes how AI sales shifted from screenshots and feature checklists to evidence-based pilots, where Fin gives customers a script, grading criteria and spreadsheet to score their last 1,000 questions over about four weeks.
moments.quote: Yeah, it has. Because of the pilots that we do and the bake-offs. Selling SaaS in the olden days was you show up with a big bag of screenshots and some feature checklists and you're like, ta-da, our product's nicer than their product.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des describes the common boomerang where customers try to build their own support agent, stall at about 44% resolution, and learn that the last stretch takes years and dozens of people.
moments.quote: There's something around the naivety of the customers. A very common thing we see a lot is people saying, I'm going to go and build my own one. We're like, okay.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Responding to Alex's Claude Code event-tech prototype, Des says a localhost app that looks done may be 3 arrows in appearance but 400 arrows from something shippable and reliable.
moments.quote: I think that's valid. Like the security, stability, reliability, like all that sort of stuff, you start to worry about them because it's one thing like to make a play app running on localhost, getting it to something that's going to like, say, withstand the crunch of a popular conference, it's actually just different.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des says replacing SaaS with internally built tools should be a deliberate strategic choice about spending engineering time, not a reaction to a quick Claude Code win.
moments.quote: And I think you'll see that happen when people and businesses move into like an extremely crunch profitability mode or whatever.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des predicts that by 2028 most customer queries will be answered instantly and accurately, changing user expectations and reducing software friction.
moments.quote: I think 2028 is probably— I think what will happen is the vast majority of customer queries will be answered instantly and accurately, and people will just come to expect that.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des says human support teams will handle the hard, messy, relationship-heavy queries in a deeper, more helpful way once AI strips away the bottom 80-90% of volume.
moments.quote: And then what does the human support do? Well, I think that what they'll be doing is frankly the hard, messy relationship building stuff. It'll be the, hey, we need to merge these 2 accounts.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des argues point solutions are no longer a sustainable business position because cheap code lets owners of the wider workflow clone and absorb them.
moments.quote: Couple of thoughts. One is like, I don't think being a point solution is a sustainable position anymore. I think you have to solve an entire problem properly end to end.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des says owners of strong systems of record like Salesforce and Workday survive, while second- or third-biggest players will be squeezed and the wedge-to-suite-to-platform strategy will fade.
moments.quote: So then that's what doesn't exist for sure. In terms of who definitely survives, anyone who owns a strong system of record, I think, still survives.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Des describes building a personal portfolio tool over three weekends to benchmark his angel investments against the S&P, gold and Bitcoin, which showed everyone made bad decisions in 2021.
moments.quote: I've definitely built software. I've built, you know, like something I care a lot about is like I invest in a lot of software companies and something I've been trying to work out is, am I actually a good investor or not?
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

moments.title: Asked what nobody asks, Des says public discourse over-indexes on AI worries and ignores the potential upside in bringing education and healthcare to billions of people.
moments.quote: In the context of press specifically, I think we are getting way too literate in ways to worry about AI and criticize AI.
moments.speaker: Des Traynor

move.text: Richard is opening up Fathom's platform so customers can take meeting data anywhere. His bet is that the data, not the software, is the asset.
move.quote: we've gone the other direction and said, no, no, we want to be the most flexible, hackable platform

numbers.text: Fathom has about 100 people, roughly 25 in engineering. The goal is $100 million ARR with fewer than 150 people.
numbers.quote: We have a pretty small engineering team. We only have, we got 100 people, about 25 of them are engineering.

broke.text: Richard's plan 18 months ago for an AIOps team building internal AI tools failed. Maintenance was terrible, so Fathom now focuses on vendor selection.
broke.quote: build a whole AIOps organization that was going to be like RevOps, build our own AI tools, whatnot. And that was a complete disaster.

advice.text: Richard tells founders to ask what they would build starting today, using their unique data and insights, and consider forking the company internally.
advice.quote: your number one job is honestly to kind of take a step back and be like, if I started from today, what would I build?

moments.title: Richard explains Fathom began as his own pain point from running sales at a prior startup, and that he saw note-taking as a problem for everyone in meetings, not just sales.
moments.quote: Like all my startups, actually, it was a problem I had at my previous startup.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard describes building Fathom in 2020 for a hypothesized future: transcription costs falling to zero and generative AI arriving, so Fathom chose the data business and built recording infrastructure first, not models.
moments.quote: Yeah, I feel like the biggest difference between this startup for me and my earlier ones is like we started Fathom with a couple of strong hypotheses about where the world was going in a couple of years.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard explains Fathom's two-value-prop model: a free, viral single-player product drives growth, while a separate manager/executive product monetizes, avoiding the trap where productivity tools have no distinct pitch to the buyer.
moments.quote: Yeah, that was the other thing that got me excited about this business is that it had a very Actually had 2 value props to 2 different people.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard lays out Fathom's three-act data strategy: viral single-player, then team sales, then a valuable organization-wide meeting dataset that users now build custom workflows on.
moments.quote: I mean, this is why I think I mentioned, like, we always thought of ourselves as a data company, right? We kind of had this 3-act play.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Fathom is opening its platform rather than hoarding transcripts, aiming to be the most flexible, hackable platform and to learn from power users to build first-class features.
moments.quote: And so, One of the big things we're leaning into, and I think it's a little unique in our space, is we're really actually opening up the platform, right?
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard says he mostly ignores competitors but credits Granola for proving the market was comfortable with client-side capture, which prompted Fathom to revisit its own product principles.
moments.quote: So, you know, I think I actually don't pay a lot of attention. I'm very kind of focused on our customers, our team. I think you can learn certain things from competition, right?
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard argues the note-taker space feels crowded to investors but less so to buyers, and that, as with Zendesk, a few hypothesis-driven early builders will endure after a rush of entrants.
moments.quote: I think for the most part though, yeah, it's gotten to be a, quote, pretty crowded space in the last year or two, but not really.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard describes Fathom's goal of $100M ARR with under 150 people, a remote, senior, small-engineering-team model that forces high leverage rather than hiring out of problems.
moments.quote: I mean, we, so one of our internal goals has always been we want to get to $100 million in revenue ARR with less than 150 people. Okay. And partially that's, we're fully remote.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard shares that Fathom's attempt to build an internal AIOps organization and custom AI tools was a disaster due to maintenance costs, so the company now focuses on centralized vendor selection and guardrails.
moments.quote: Obviously, there's a lot of stuff around making it easy for people to pick up AI tools, which ones to pick up and not use.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard argues that while creating software has become cheaper, maintaining it hasn't, and the LLM treadmill of short-lived models makes bespoke internal tools costly, so SaaS remains viable though expectations rise.
moments.quote: It's funny because there's a lot of concern about what's going to happen to SaaS with AI, but what's going to— SaaS, one of the big pitches of SaaS, it's not that expensive.
moments.speaker: Richard White

moments.title: Richard advises established SaaS founders to ask what they would build starting today, identify their unique data and insights, consider forking the company internally, and avoid bolt-on AI because software is a liability while data and insights are the assets.
moments.quote: I think your number one job is honestly to kind of take a step back and be like, if I started from today, what would I build? Yeah.
moments.speaker: Richard White

move.text: Marty optimises for growth, not efficiency. Pylon treats AI as an accelerant and is still hiring for 30 open roles.
move.quote: Here's what I'd say is like, I do not optimize for efficiency at all. I'm optimizing for growth.

numbers.text: Almost 30 engineers using Cursor and Claude Code saw a 40% productivity lift over five months, not the 4x or 5x some expect.
numbers.quote: we've had a 40% lift in engineering productivity over the course of like 5 months

broke.text: Turning up at conferences without targets failed. One New York event yielded about four demos for six staff, prompting a 50-demo target and 10-demo personal quotas.
broke.quote: Like I remember we went to one conference in New York and we booked maybe like 4 demos.

advice.text: Marty tells founders not to chase AI for its own sake. Ask how to 10x, and tie every decision back to revenue.
advice.quote: So I would ask that question, always tie it back to revenue because that should be the goal and that should be the outcome.

moments.title: Marty explains why Pylon's early conference approach of paying, showing up and hoping failed, and how they fixed it by picking the right people and setting quotas and incentives like any sales team.
moments.quote: Yeah, so it's actually pretty simple. So we did what everyone did at past conferences. And this was before we had an events marketer.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty shows how to work backwards from demos to qualified opportunities to revenue, and compare that to event and opportunity costs, to set a profitable conference goal.
moments.quote: So what we did was we looked at our past conferences. We're like, okay, like. How many people realistically do we think we can book based on attendee count that we expect?
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Pylon set a 50-demo goal with a 10-demo personal quota and a team reward, and Marty notes that most other booths had no goal, target or incentive.
moments.quote: And so we said, okay, we want to book 50 demos with people here. And we told the team in advance and we also told them, each of you have a quota of 10 people each, 10 demos.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty describes Pylon as the AI-native, B2B-focused alternative to Zendesk or Intercom, centralizing customer context that is scattered across calls, emails and Slack.
moments.quote: So Pylon is the first AI customer support platform built for B2B companies. So the easiest way to think about this is if you're already using a ticketing system like a Zendesk or an Intercom or a Salesforce Service Cloud, we are the AI-native version of those products, but specifically focused on a B2B use case.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty argues that money or a personally experienced problem are poor motivations for a company that takes ten years to build.
moments.quote: Yeah, so our motivation for starting a company is purely fun. very different answer than most people. A lot of people are like money or like I had this problem and I wanted to solve it.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty outlines Pylon's early go-to-market sequence: crawl the personal network, then send 30-40 customized LinkedIn DMs a day during YC, then lean into organic build-in-public content.
moments.quote: And then the next couple were One was a former coworker of one of my co-founders had started a company, and so we sold into them. Another was someone who had tried to hire my third co-founder.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty says Pylon's first $8-10 million in revenue largely came from organic LinkedIn storytelling that worked like a real-time TV show, and authentic details like earning minimum wage stuck with people.
moments.quote: And we've been doing that for the past 3 years. And actually a lot of our customers, especially early on, probably our first like $8 to $10 million came from organic LinkedIn content where people just like fell in love with the story.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty gives a reality check: Pylon's roughly 30 engineers use Cursor and Claude Code aggressively, yet measured engineering productivity rose about 40% over five months, not 4-5x.
moments.quote: I think it's really cultural, to be honest. I was talking to someone here, a CFO, and they were talking about how their team— they have their engineering team in Europe and they're scared of using AI because they're like, hey, this might replace us or like might reduce our need.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty frames AI to the team as an accelerant that expands the pie and market, so Pylon is still hiring engineers and SDRs, with about 30 open roles.
moments.quote: And I think it's just, you're limited by the bandwidth of like Hey, when you are building software, there are only so many decisions you can make or like context that you can hold.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty says he does not optimize for efficiency but for growth, and pushes back on prospects who claim they can vibe code Pylon's product when a 100-person team using the same frontier models already works on it daily.
moments.quote: Here's what I'd say is like, I do not optimize for efficiency at all. I'm optimizing for growth.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

moments.title: Marty's advice on AI strategy: skip the list of AI experiments, ask how you can 10x or make the most money right now, and tie every decision back to revenue.
moments.quote: I mean, I just look at where's the opportunity, right? Literally, just ask yourself, like, how can we make the most money right now? And I bet you it's something related to AI.
moments.speaker: Marty Kausas

move.text: Paul chose venture capital over bootstrapping for speed and capitalisation. Less well-capitalised rivals in revenue-based financing died along the way.
move.quote: the main reason for us to do this as a venture-backed case was the conviction that speed and capitalization matters.

numbers.text: Event research that took two juniors a full week now takes a good prompt and two hours. Automated credit memos save about two days per deal.
numbers.quote: Historically, 2 juniors working on a larger event for, I don't know, a full week compared to a good prompt and 2 hours.

broke.text: The growth-quality tension never resolves. Paul still negotiates hard with lenders and tells VCs that tripling must be good enough instead of quadrupling.
broke.quote: you can't avoid having some tough discussions and negotiate hard and explain to refinancing parties why that way is the right one

advice.text: Paul tells founders to audit gross margin honestly, fund R&D with equity and fund acquisition costs that pay back in 6 to 9 months with debt.
advice.quote: take a look at your P&L, take a look at the figures that you report, and just look at the cost items

moments.title: Paul pitches re:cap as the first place a SaaS founder should think of when they need non-dilutive capital, whether they know what they need or not.
moments.quote: Imagine you're a SaaS founder and you need some capital and you don't want to give up equity for it. Then we want to be the first place that pops up in your mind.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul explains he is not a banker and fell into fintech by accident, moving from a university investing club to a micro-investing firm that became Liqid and eventually re:cap.
moments.quote: So I'm not a banker. I've never been a banker. It really— the honest answer, it happened by accident. It was at university. The investing club we had there, that was the first exposure I had to finance.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul challenges the 'woke up and wanted to change the world' founder narrative, saying founders are made by being crazy enough to keep going despite early naysayers.
moments.quote: I mean, I couldn't agree more. You oftentimes hear these PR stories where founders say, you know, I woke up in the morning and then I had that thought how I will change the world.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul explains that after experiencing both VC-backed and bootstrapped companies, re:cap chose venture backing because speed and capitalization matter, noting under-capitalized competitors died.
moments.quote: Yeah, I mean, first of all, I must confess, the first company that we started, we didn't think about that at all. For the first company, we were just excited.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says re:cap's debt product wasn't why it took VC money; different funding instruments suit different purposes, and re:cap doesn't tell founders never to raise equity.
moments.quote: And on your comment, that we are somewhat an alternative to venture capital, or our product offers an alternative to that.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul describes the core challenge of a lending startup: VCs push for maximum growth while debt investors want quality, granularity and liquidity, and companies have failed by growing too fast or too cautiously.
moments.quote: I think the real interesting challenge in building up such a company is that you need to balance interests of 2 very different stakeholders.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says re:cap recognized the conflict on day one and manages it through tough negotiations with refinancing parties and by resetting VC expectations from quadrupling to tripling.
moments.quote: And what did we do differently? I would say That conflict was clear on day one, and we just tried our best to balance it.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says the capital-efficiency era and tougher equity markets drove founders to look for alternatives and increased demand for re:cap.
moments.quote: I mean, to the first part of the question, you already answered it yourself. Like, capital efficiency was suddenly a very hot topic. Everybody was talking about burn multiples.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul contrasts SaaS firms using AI to work more efficiently with products that embed AI deeply and see gross margins fall from 85% to 50-60%, noting both can still raise equity.
moments.quote: Fast forward to today, I would say it really depends on where you sit across the spectrum as an AI company.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says SaaSpocalypse hasn't changed re:cap's thinking because it has always favored B2B SaaS deeply integrated into customer processes, which gives more time to respond to AI.
moments.quote: Has SaaSpocalypse had such a meaningful impact on how we think about what companies should be financed or not?
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says gross margin is just one input to credit decisions alongside integration depth, that no one knows which AI models will work in 5 years, and that structured debt can mitigate change in a way equity cannot.
moments.quote: In the end, the short answer to that is obviously gross margin is not everything that drives a credit decision. It's one of many aspects.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul explains re:cap has used machine learning since founding for structuring and enriching data, still prefers it to LLMs for cost and accuracy on huge volumes of bank transactions, but expects LLMs to take over.
moments.quote: Yeah. So we work with AI in our product since we started the company, but old school AI, I shall say. So machine learning. In that context, we mostly use AI for structuring and enriching data.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says the biggest wow moment was using AI in re:cap's own non-engineering workflows over the last 3-6 months, more than seeing the product's capabilities.
moments.quote: Lastly, and that is probably— might be a bit counterintuitive, but I actually heard similar stories from other founders as well. The last thing where we actually heavily started to use AI is in our own workflows.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says lending remains a relationship game because founders want a reliable partner, so AI should free people to do work that deserves human attention.
moments.quote: Yeah, you already named the most crucial aspect. Still a relationship game. Again, I was actually surprised to learn this previously when we were working on Liquid, like a wealth management company.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul describes Capital AI as an embedded LLM with context on a company's connected financials, plus agentic monitoring that gives founders peace of mind.
moments.quote: In the end, it's an embedded LLM into our platform that has access to all the data that you as a company have connected to our platform that we have already structured and enriched.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul predicts more early-stage companies will use debt funding by 2028, tempered by uncertainty over media backlash and institutional appetite.
moments.quote: When I get questions like this, historically, what I would've always said, and actually I would still say it today, is My projection is more early-stage companies will use debt funding, and we see that clearly more companies do this today than they used to do it like 3 years ago.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says re:cap keeps a long-term vision and strategy with trial-and-error execution, even as AI's pace makes him question how much long-term planning is worth.
moments.quote: So we internally still operate under the same principle, which basically is there must be a vision, a very long-term vision, and there must be a strategy that we believe can bring us to that vision.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul advises a $3M ARR, VC-funded SaaS founder to verify their real gross margin, then review each P&L cost item, using equity for R&D and considering debt for acquisition costs that pay back in 6-9 months.
moments.quote: So first of all, I would challenge that person. Does she or he really have 90% gross margin? And do a calculation on that and be honest to yourself.
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Paul says the unasked question in financing is the emotional cost of a bad decision, citing founders who accepted high liquidation preferences or raised too much and feel stuck.
moments.quote: The thing about what I think people oftentimes don't ask or never I've actually never been publicly asked about this, but I do think it's relevant in the context of what we are doing at Recap, is what is actually the emotional cost of a bad financing or funding decision?
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

moments.title: Asked in one sentence whether AI is killing SaaS, Paul answers 'Absolutely not.'
moments.quote: I'm sure many of them are going to be asking, is AI killing their business?
moments.speaker: Paul Becker

move.text: Roy changed monday.com's vision from managing work to doing it. Seats stay for people and agents; consumption pricing is added for the work itself.
move.quote: we shifted that vision to being not only manage work but also doing the work.

numbers.text: monday.com has 250,000 paying customers and millions of users across more than 200 industries.
numbers.quote: maybe it's worth mentioning Monday right now has like 250,000 paying companies, paying customers and millions of users.

broke.text: After February's sell-off and a pulled 2027 target, Roy admits agent seat purchases are not yet significant.
broke.quote: we have agents signing up and purchasing seats on the platform, but it's not significant, okay?

advice.text: Roy went back to writing code himself. He tells founders to understand the technology deeply and get an autonomous agent working for them now.
advice.quote: But the main thing, understand the technology, go deep, open an OpenCLAW right now, you know, and try and make it work for you.

moments.title: Roy explains monday.com began by solving the broad problem of how people work together rather than project management, which kept it wide across 200+ industries.
moments.quote: Yeah. So when we started, it was Wix was the first customer. And I think we started with an interesting problem, which was like, how do people work together? Not how do we manage projects?
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy explains monday.com's broad ICP worked because of zero-complexity configurability, and recommends considering three ICPs rather than entrenching in one narrow path.
moments.quote: Yeah, so I think like we had an ICP, it was just not— it was addressable in a very non-addressable way, which was like people who really want to manage stuff well.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy describes how the Depulse name held adoption back, how objections and internal pressure arose, and how reframing the rebrand as a simple rename released fears.
moments.quote: Yeah, so it was working in a way that we had success before we changed the name, but it wasn't working and it was easy for us to switch a name because like people like told us every day, I'm not introducing this to my team because of the name, you know?
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy recounts how an investor suggested the name Monday, which he embraced because it carries emotions about work that the company aims to change.
moments.quote: So we were trying to replace the name for like a year and then one of our investors came and told me, you know, I have a name for the company.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy explains the co-CEO relationship with Eran runs on investing in trust and shared context, and that the key is walking the path together rather than getting what he wants.
moments.quote: So I think it's like a relationship. Really, we talk about it like a relationship. We invest in the relationship and I know a lot of couple CEOs don't.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy characterizes the stock decline as a sector-wide SaaS repricing driven by investor uncertainty over who will adapt, not a monday.com-specific event.
moments.quote: Yeah. So it wasn't the first drop we had. Like, the first drop was like a 2 years ago when the whole market dropped and I kind of feel the same way about this situation, which means we didn't drop alone.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy argues software must shift from managing work to doing the work, with consumption pricing for AI work and seats retained for people and agents, and the software pie growing bigger.
moments.quote: So I think like there's a lot of changes that has to happen with SaaS. One of them is not relying solely on the seat model.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy admits agent signups are not yet significant, calling it a classic innovator's dilemma where a small niche will grow into a massive market.
moments.quote: Yeah, so we have agents signing up and purchasing seats on the platform, but it's not significant, okay? Why? Because that's how markets evolve, you know?
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy lays out three waves of AI and recounts his moment of clarity when an AI coding agent pushed back on building a third feature, acting like a true partner.
moments.quote: so I really see the AI changes like 3 waves. The first wave was ChatGPT when it was introduced.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy says the first step in adapting is organizational mindset change, after which monday.com quickly shipped agents, monday vibe, and Sidekick.
moments.quote: Yeah, so I think like we need to talk like a step back and talk about the organizational change, the mind shift change. Yeah.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy disagrees with the burn-it-down approach, arguing a growing company should bring its existing customers into the AI era while building new AI-native offerings like Agent Talent, bridging the gap where AI adoption and token ROI remain low.
moments.quote: Yeah. So I think like that's the tricky part. If you have a massive user base that rely on you and want to use your product and are using it, you need to bring them also to the new world.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy advises SaaS founders to go deep on the technology themselves, noting that the core customer problem may remain but how it is solved will change, and to open OpenClaw now and make it work for them.
moments.quote: So I can share what I did. I did like I didn't write code for a long while and I actually think they threw a party when they threw the last line of code from the system that I wrote, you know, but I'm back to coding a lot because I want to understand the technology deeply and I find that it's very important because then I can drive change and then I can move us to a new place.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

moments.title: Roy challenges the 'SaaS is dead because seats vanish' narrative by noting that vanishing seats imply vanishing jobs, urging people to think more deeply about contradictory assumptions.
moments.quote: Well, they ask so, like, so many different questions. Like, I'll tell you what I think people are not doing enough. Which is thinking more deeply into their assumptions.
moments.speaker: Roy Mann

move.text: Nicolas is betting on platforms over point solutions. Attio pairs a flexible data layer with automation built for agents running go-to-market.
move.quote: And so we're very bullish on platforms. We're very bullish on consolidation, actually.

numbers.text: Nicolas says writing code is only about 15% of a scaled software company's budget. Attio runs millions of automations a day.
numbers.quote: It's maybe 15% of their budget would be considered as being spent on actually writing code.

broke.text: Nicolas admits he did not look after himself in the early years. He calls the overwork wrong and detrimental.
broke.quote: when we were 5 people in a coworking space for multiple years, the answer is I kind of didn't.

advice.text: Nicolas tells founders with a few million in ARR to face AI honestly and start experimenting with the tools now.
advice.quote: start experimenting, start using the tools, start building things, start living at the edge of what's capable

moments.title: Nicolas explains how Attio grew organically from a simple tool he built as a VC to check whether anyone in the fund had already spoken to a contact, which later became a side project that gained traction and led him into CRM.
moments.quote: But where it really started was I worked in VC, and while I was working in VC, I had a thesis that we could be doing more with our email and calendar.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas says modern AI tools would have sped up his early bootstrapped building, but expectations have risen so much that the old version wouldn't cut it, because easier building means doing more rather than doing the same with less.
moments.quote: Yes, a lot would have changed. I mean, the Well, Attio, the previous company I started before that, Funstack, were bootstrapped at the beginning. And that bootstrapping phase was slow.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas explains that disbelief that Salesforce didn't carry modern product philosophy, plus theses on malleability and high-resolution data, tipped Attio into taking on the category, and that naivety helped because outsiders aren't scared off by knowing too much.
moments.quote: And the driving force for us was a little bit of disbelief that in a world of really good software and really good tools, that the biggest one and the most successful one was Salesforce.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas argues the AI-native versus legacy distinction isn't very helpful; what matters is whether a product's architecture handles data, context and governance and can adapt quickly, citing Replit and Clay as non-AI-native winners.
moments.quote: Yeah. So I think there are— I'm not sure how helpful the AI-native versus not AI-native distinction is, because there are going to be some incredible companies in the AI era that were not born AI-native, and companies that we already can see have amazing traction.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas says companies shouldn't rebuild mission-critical tools like their CRM with AI, because young companies should pour their brainpower into their own product rather than problems others have already solved.
moments.quote: Yeah, people will do that. I don't think it's the right thing to do.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas argues code generation is only a small part of building software, since data security, scalability and content matter too, and most vibe-coded alternatives would have been nice five years ago but aren't where the puck is going.
moments.quote: So that's one aspect of it. The other aspect is that code generation is a small part of building a product.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas explains where vibe coding does belong: internal tools where no good solution exists, away from mission-critical customer data, and last-mile customization built on top of platforms like Attio's SDK.
moments.quote: Now, I still think there is an incredible space for vibe coding in companies, and we build a lot of software for internal consumption.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Alex shares how a SaaStock colleague returning from maternity leave, with no knowledge of Lovable, built a long-missing community product feature in three weeks.
moments.quote: You know, SaaStock is not a software company. We serve the B2B software market.
moments.speaker: Alex Theuma

moments.title: Nicolas names Claude Code as his favorite vibe-coding tool because of his engineering background, while Attio lets its team choose among v0, Replit and Lovable as the tool leaderboard constantly shifts.
moments.quote: Are you using or testing all the vibe coding platforms? Lovable, Replit, Claude Code? Do you have a favorite? I have a favorite. For me, it's Claude Code.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas says AI is largely killing SaaS as we knew it but not software itself: expectations are shifting to autonomous, highly customizable products, many companies won't adapt, and new winners will emerge in a do-or-die paradigm shift.
moments.quote: Yeah. So the first thing was, is AI killing SaaS? I think the answer to that is yes, to a large degree it is.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas says SaaS had become formulaic and incremental, and now that nobody knows the answers, building software is more interesting and motivating.
moments.quote: Yeah, but it's good because this is kind of— I sort of— the reason that people, a lot of people get into software is because they like building things, they like creating things.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas says AI-driven headcount cuts are overblown and often air cover for fixing bloated organizations, because investors now demand either real profit or hypergrowth and slowing companies find cutting easier than accelerating.
moments.quote: No, we're very much not stop hiring. I think that it's overblown, and I think in most cases it's really good air cover for fixing other organizational problems.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas says running growth marketing with one person plus agents is plausible, but Anthropic will still grow its marketing department because expectations of output rise an order of magnitude.
moments.quote: No, I don't. I don't think that's PR. I think that, I think that you could absolutely run a You could run growth marketing with one person.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas states Attio's thesis that B2B go-to-market systems will become autonomous, designed and monitored by humans but able to run and scale on their own.
moments.quote: But fundamentally, we have, you know, we have, we have a thesis on this, which is that It's going to be extremely important, especially when we think about how we position Attio in the market.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas explains why autonomous operations favor consolidated data-rich platforms with transactionally consistent automations, and why narrowly scoped point solutions are being absorbed.
moments.quote: In that world, I think platforms become really important, and it becomes really important that you have a platform that is able to kind of store all the data that you need, that has all the context that you need, and importantly, that is malleable enough to actually mould to what you're trying to do.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas advises established SaaS founders to confront the AI shift honestly, accept it, and reframe it as one of the biggest opportunities, using the grit that built their company.
moments.quote: Yeah, I mean, I think the thing is to just confront the situation in the most honest way that you can, which is that not thinking about it or ignoring it, et cetera, it doesn't change anything, right?
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas describes Attio's Particle data layer, a highly scalable, flexible object model that can map any business, plus universal context that adds embeddings for free and makes Attio a context engine for agents.
moments.quote: The big thing for us is the depth that we have gone to to build the data layer and the automation layer on top. And marrying these things super closely together is what provides all the value.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas explains Attio's automation layer, which lets teams slide between fully deterministic workflows like forecasting and probabilistic ones for messy communication data, running millions of automations.
moments.quote: And then the next thing is the automation layer on top. And there's a lot of very cool things we're about to announce.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp

moments.title: Nicolas shares his resilience practice for founder highs and lows: don't react to "it's all over" or "we'll crush it" moments, give yourself a week on autopilot, and the perspective will change.
moments.quote: There is one thing that I did do which was really helpful, which is that you have these massive ups and downs, and there are times when something happens and you think, we're going to absolutely crush it.
moments.speaker: Nicolas Sharp
